reviewer_rebuttals.response: Concern: leakage and split validity. Clarification: Augmentation used only training commits (4.4.2: “generate two paraphrases for each training commit”), and the held-out test split was never used for model selection (4.4.3). We acknowledge that we did not describe leakage controls sufficiently and that our 80/20 split on augmented data for validation could be clearer. Changes: (i) corpus-level de-duplication before splitting; (ii) semantic similarity filtering of synthetic data against dev/test; (iii) validation drawn only from the original training set; (iv) fixed seeds and repository-/time-aware splits added as robustness checks. We will report both random-stratified and repo/time-holdout results (without claiming new numbers here). We will release commit/message IDs for all splits.

Concern: biased zero-shot setup and mapping validity. We agree our lexicon-based override for Caution may bias comparisons; we have removed it and now use a uniform protocol. Revisions to §4.2: (i) multiple prompt templates per model with majority vote; (ii) standardized hypothesis templates for MNLI; (iii) consistent preprocessing across models; (iv) explicit label mapping tables; (v) no test-time calibration or threshold tuning; (vi) report random and majority-class baselines and confidence intervals. We will include all prompts, mappings, and scripts in the artifact to ensure reproduci bility and fair zero-shot comparisons.

Concern: missing ablations and insufficient reproducibility detail. We concur. Revisions: We add an ablation plan isolating each factor: (a) CodeBERT on gold only; (b) +backtranslation; (c) +off-the-shelf LLaMA paraphrases; (d) +fine-tuned LLaMA paraphrases; (e) synthetic-only; (f) mixing ratios and loss weighting; (g) number of paraphrases; (h) removal of potential near-duplicates. We will report per-class metrics, 95% bootstrap CIs, and McNemar tests vs. the primary baseline. We also add exact preprocessing, split IDs, seeds, and training scripts, plus annotation guidelines and reconciliation rules for full reproducibility.

revised_sections.content:
All experiments use the 2,000-message gold-standard dataset with a fixed held-out test split of 400 examples; the remaining 1,600 form the training pool. A validation set is drawn exclusively from the training pool and used for early stopping and model selection; the test set is never used for tuning.
Leakage controls. Before splitting, we perform corpus-level de-duplication (exact-match and normalized variants). Synthetic data are generated only from training messages. We filter synthetic outputs that are near-duplicates of any dev/test message (semantic similarity and hash-based checks) and remove duplicates within the training set. We fix random seeds and will release split IDs for full reproducibility. In addition to stratified random splits, we report robustness checks with (i) repository-holdout and (ii) temporally separated splits (train earlier, test later) to assess generalization under distribution shift.
Metrics and statistics. We report Macro-F1, per-class precision/recall/F1, and accuracy. We provide 95% bootstrap confidence intervals and conduct McNemar tests for paired comparisons to the primary baseline. All preprocessing, training, and evaluation scripts (including seed control) will be released in an anonymized artifact.
Baselines. We evaluate five pretrained models spanning general-purpose reasoning, code-aware representation, and emotion-focused classification (as listed previously). We ensure identical preprocessing across models and no heuristic overrides.
Fine-tuning. For fine-tuned baselines, the classification head is a four-way softmax. Early stopping and model selection use the validation set only. Hyperparameters and seeds are fixed and documented in the artifact.

We evaluate all baselines in a uniform zero-shot framework without any heuristic overrides. For RoBERTa-large-MNLI, we pair each commit (premise) with standardized hypothesis templates (e.g., “This commit expresses {label}.”) and select the label with the highest entailment score; we also include logically equivalent variants and aggregate by majority vote. For emotion-tuned classifiers, we map fine-grained emotions to our four labels using an explicit, published mapping table. For generative models, we use an ensemble of prompt templates instructing four-class classification; outputs are normalized and aggregated by majority vote.
No component is tuned on the test set, and prompts/templates are fixed prior to evaluation. We report performance with identical preprocessing across models, alongside random and majority-class baselines and 95% CIs. All prompts, mappings, and normalization scripts will be released.

CommiTune is a two-stage pipeline: (1) fine-tune a generative LLaMA model on the 1,600 training commits to align with the four-label taxonomy; (2) use it to synthesize paraphrases only for training commits, then fine-tune CodeBERT on the union of gold and filtered synthetic data.
Stage 1 (generator fine-tuning). We adapt Meta-LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct using PEFT/LoRA. Training uses the 1,600 training commits, a four-way output space, and early stopping on the validation set; no test information is used. Exact seeds and configuration are provided in the artifact.
Stage 2 (augmentation and filtering). For each training commit, the generator produces paraphrases conditioned on the gold label. We then: (i) remove duplicates and enforce single-sentence formatting; (ii) discard outputs whose semantic similarity to the seed is too low (to avoid label drift) or too high (to avoid trivial copies); (iii) filter out any synthetic instance that is near-duplicate to any dev/test message (to prevent leakage). We upweight gold data during training via sampling/loss weighting (documented in the artifact).
Final training. CodeBERT is fine-tuned on the combined dataset with early stopping on the validation set drawn from gold data. Seeds, hyperparameters, and training scripts are fixed and released.
Ablations and controls. We will report: CodeBERT on gold only; +backtranslation; +off-the-shelf LLaMA paraphrases; +fine-tuned LLaMA paraphrases; synthetic-only; varying the number of paraphrases and mixing policies; and removal of potential near-duplicates. We include per-class metrics, 95% CIs, and McNemar tests versus the gold-only baseline.

key_changes: Removed the lexicon-based override and standardized a fair, model-agnostic zero-shot protocol with prompt ensembles and explicit mappings.
Added rigorous leakage controls: corpus-level de-duplication, semantic filtering against dev/test, fixed seeds, and repository/time-aware robustness splits.
Clarified train/validation/test usage, with early stopping only on validation derived from training and no test-time tuning.
Specified a comprehensive ablation suite isolating augmentation source, quantity, and mixing, with confidence intervals and statistical tests.
Committed to releasing anonymized code, prompts, split IDs, seeds, and annotation guidelines to ensure full reproducibility.

response_payload.summary: Q-RAG fine-tunes a retriever embedder with value-based RL for multi-step retrieval, using state/action embedders with (relative) RoPE and a PQN-style TD learner. It targets ultra-long contexts and reports SOTA on BabiLong and RULER, with competitive HotPotQA/MuSiQue results, while training on a single A100. An inner-product theory (App. A) supports the scoring class; early-stopping analysis is provided.
response_payload.significance_and_novelty: Training the embedder (not the LLM) with value-based RL for multi-step retrieval is a useful efficiency-oriented twist, and the relative positional scheme for temporal reasoning is interesting. Novelty is moderate vis-à-vis RePlug/BeamRetriever/RL-agent lines.
reasons_for_acceptance: Section 3.2: A clear, efficient value-based formulation with state/action embedders and dot-product Q enables scalable multi-step retrieval.
Section 3.3: The relative position encoding tied to already-selected facts is a neat, well-motivated addition for temporal/narrative tasks.
Section 4.3–4.4 and App. B: Early-stopping analysis and OOD MuSiQue results indicate some robustness beyond in-distribution tuning.
Appendix D,G: Complexity analysis and practical training details (single A100) make the approach attractive for practitioners.
reasons_for_rejection: Section 3.2 mischaracterizes Appendix A as providing “convergence guarantees,” but App. A contains approximation results for inner-product classes, not RL convergence, weakening the theoretical claim.
Section 5 (Table 3) ablation values are missing (shown as “. ± .”), preventing verification of the benefit of Soft-Q, target networks, and RL vs SFT, which directly affects claimed contributions.

Section 4.2–4.3: Central SOTA claims rely heavily on reported numbers from disparate setups; Table 1 is incomplete and unclear (missing columns/entries), impeding a fair, controlled comparison at ICLR standards.

Clarity issues throughout (e.g., missing equations around soft Q definitions in §3.2, broken tables/figures, numerous formatting/grammar issues) reduce confidence in correctness and reproducibility despite the code link.
suggestions: Appendix D: Add a wall-clock throughput/memory comparison against BeamRetriever and ANN-backed retrieval with and without PQN to substantiate efficiency claims.
Section 3.3: Provide an explicit ablation isolating absolute vs relative positional indexing to quantify temporal-reasoning gains.
Section 4.4: Report results with a standard public answerer and decoding settings to ease comparison, and include sensitivity to retrieval budget on HotPotQA/MuSiQue in the main text.
Appendix G: Release evaluation scripts that compute Fact EM/F1 exactly as defined, plus seeds and data splits, to align with open-review scrutiny.

response_payload.summary: The paper proposes Q-RAG, a value-based RL method that fine-tunes a retriever’s embedder for multi-step RAG. It builds on PQN with soft-Q and target networks and a factorized Q for scalable selection. Experiments on BabiLong, RULER (NIAH), HotPotQA, and MuSiQue show strong long-context generalization (up to 1M tokens) and competitive open-domain QA, including best OOD MuSiQue. Ablations support design choices.
response_payload.significance_and_novelty: Applies on-policy value-based RL (PQN + soft-Q + targets) to train a retriever, addressing replay-buffer issues and scaling to long contexts, with empirical SOTA on long-context stress tests and strong OOD QA; novelty is incremental relative to prior RL-tuned retrievers.
reasons_for_acceptance: Section 3.2 introduces a clear value-based RL formulation (PQN with soft value functions and target networks) and a factorized Q scoring, addressing replay-buffer inefficiency in large action spaces.
Section 4.3/Table 1 shows near-perfect NIAH and generalization from training at 4K to evaluation at 1M tokens without accuracy loss.
Section 4.4 and Appendix E report strong open-domain QA, matching Search-R1 and outperforming alternatives on MuSiQue OOD; Plan Q-RAG performs similarly.
Section 5 ablations (with three seeds) indicate benefits of soft-Q and target networks and analyze sensitivity to λ and α.
reasons_for_rejection: Section 4.4 claims Q-RAG “surpasses all other baselines on HotPotQA,” but Appendix E shows Beam Retriever slightly higher on HotPotQA (Ans F1 0.77 vs 0.76; Ans EM 0.61 vs 0.59; Fact metrics), making the claim overstated.
Section 4.4 states baseline numbers were taken from prior papers, and G (Evaluation Details) uses QwQ-32B only for some methods; generator/config mismatches undermine apples-to-apples comparisons.
G (Fact-level metrics) defines Fact EM as gt⊆pred, which does not penalize extra irrelevant chunks and can overstate retrieval quality when predictions are long.
Section 5 ablations are confined to BabiLong-QA3; there is no ablation on open-domain QA to show that soft-Q/targets consistently drive gains there.
suggestions: Add qualitative analyses of retrieval trajectories and typical failure modes to illuminate what the value function learns (Section 3.2/Appendix C).
Report sensitivity to the retrieval step limit T across datasets beyond BabiLong (G Evaluation Details).
Summarize the main assumptions and theorem statements from Appendix A in the main text (Section 3.2) to improve accessibility.
Release code and training scripts to facilitate reproducibility of the multi-seed ablations (Section 5/G).

response_payload.summary: The paper proposes Q-RAG, a multi-step retrieval method that trains the embedder with value-based TD reinforcement learning and a temporal chunk-position encoding, targeting long-context and multi-hop QA. It reports strong results on BabiLong QA3 and RULER, and competitive HotPotQA/MuSiQue performance, with ablations on Soft-Q/target networks and early stopping. Code and checkpoints are released; training fits on a single A100.
response_payload.significance_and_novelty: Training the retriever via TD-RL with a temporal encoding is novel relative to SFT/agentic multi-step RAG and beam retrievers, and the claimed ultra-long-context generalization is potentially impactful if validated.
reasons_for_acceptance: Sec. 4.2 reports strong, stable performance on BabiLong QA3 across increasing context length where competing long-context methods degrade.
Sec. 4.4 and App. E show competitive fact/answer scores on HotPotQA and OOD MuSiQue, matching Search-R1 and approaching Beam Retriever without LLM fine-tuning.
Sec. 5 ablations (Table 3, Fig. 3) indicate the necessity of Soft-Q, target networks, λ-return and entropy regularization, supporting the methodological choices.
Reproducibility statement and App. G provide code, checkpoints, hyperparameters, and consistent generation settings, suggesting the work is replicable on a single A100.
reasons_for_rejection: Abstract and Sec. 4.3 conflict on context length claims ("up to 10M tokens" vs experiments shown up to 1M), and no table/figure for 10M was available to verify the SOTA claim.

Sec. 4.4 states baseline numbers were taken from papers and Sec. 4.1 notes resource limits, while App. G uses QwQ-32B for answers in our runs, creating potential evaluation non-comparability with reported baselines that may use different generators.
Sec. 3.1 indicates all experiments rely on support-fact supervision rather than answer-level rewards, which limits applicability to settings lacking annotated supporting facts.

Sec. 3.3 outlines a temporal positional encoding but omits a precise formulation and complexity analysis, and Appendix A introduces a Q-function approximation framework whose practical role in the implementation is unclear.
suggestions: App. G: add sensitivity analyses to chunk size and sentence-boundary handling to document robustness beyond the chosen fixed segmentation.
Sec. 3.3: include qualitative case studies visualizing temporal decisions over S_t to illustrate how temporal encoding guides retrieval.
Sec. B: report the distribution of stopping times and threshold calibration curves across datasets to aid deployment tuning.

response_payload.summary: Reviewers agree Q-RAG’s value-based RL for training a retriever is promising, efficient, and strong on long-context tasks, with competitive open-domain QA and solid OOD MuSiQue results. They also concur that clarity and rigor are lacking: broken/omitted equations and ablation values, an overstated theory claim, and non-comparable baselines/metrics undermine SOTA claims (e.g., HotPotQA). The 10M-token claim is unsubstantiated. Overall, promising but needs fixes and cleaner evaluation.

Strong long-context results on BabiLong/RULER and competitive open-domain QA with robust OOD MuSiQue are consistent across reviews.
Presentation issues are substantial, including missing equations, broken tables/figures, and ablation values that block verification.
Baseline comparability and metric design (e.g., generator mismatches and permissive Fact EM) weaken SOTA claims, including on HotPotQA.

revised_sections.content:
We perform multi-step retrieval with a value-based, maximum-entropy RL agent. For a policy π, the soft value functions (Ziebart, 2010; Haarnoja et al., 2018) satisfy the soft Bellman relations:
(1)  Vπ(s) = α · log ∑_{a∈A(s)} exp(Qπ(s,a)/α)
(2)  Qπ(s,a) = r(s,a) + γ · E_{s'∼p(·|s,a)}[ Vπ(s') ]
with temperature α>0 controlling exploration. We use the corresponding Boltzmann policy
(3)  πθ(a|s) = exp(Qθ(s,a)/α) / ∑_{a'∈A(s)} exp(Qθ(s,a')/α).

Q-function parameterization. We approximate Q with separate embedders for states and actions:
(4)  Qθ(s,a_i) = ⟨ Es(s;θ1), Ea(a_i,i;θ2) ⟩,
where Es, Ea ∈ ℝ^d, ⟨·,·⟩ is the inner product, and Ea encodes chunk content and its index i via rotary/relative positional features. This low-cost factorization avoids per-candidate transformer scoring.

Soft state value. Given Qθ, we compute the soft state value with a target network θ′ for stability:
(5)  Vθ′(s) = α · log ∑_{a∈A(s)} exp(Qθ′(s,a)/α).

Training target. For a trajectory (s_t,a_t,r_t,s_{t+1})_{t=1..T}, we use λ-returns with soft bootstrapping:
(6)  G_{t:t+n} = ∑_{k=1}^{n} γ^{k-1} r_{t+k} + γ^n Vθ′(s_{t+n})
(7)  G_t^λ = (1−λ) ∑_{n=1}^{T−t} λ^{n−1} G_{t:t+n} + λ^{T−t} G_{t:T},
where λ∈[0,1]. The critic minimizes the MSE:
(8)  L(θ) = (1/T) ∑_{t=1}^{T} ( Qθ(s_t,a_t) − G_t^λ )^2.

Target updates and temperature. Target parameters are updated by EMA: θ′ ← τθ + (1−τ)θ′. We linearly anneal α from an initial value to 0 during training (proportional to the learning rate), yielding a near-greedy policy at convergence while preserving early exploration.

On-policy backbone. We adopt PQN (Gallici et al., 2024) as the temporal-difference backbone to avoid replay and repeated re-embedding of long documents. Our departures from the original PQN are: (i) soft value functions (Eqs. 1–3) and (ii) target networks (Eq. 5). Both stabilize training in our large action spaces.

Action set and STOP. At step t, A_t contains all chunks not yet selected plus a special STOP action. Episodes end when STOP is chosen or when the budget T is reached. The transition is deterministic: s_{t+1} = ord([q, a_0, …, a_t]).

Algorithmic sketch. For each episode: (a) embed all chunks once with Ea; (b) at each step, compute Es(s_t), evaluate Qθ(s_t,·) by dot products, sample a_t via Eq. (3), record r_t, and update the state; (c) compute Vθ′(s_t) via Eq. (5); (d) build λ-returns with Eq. (7); (e) update θ by minimizing Eq. (8); (f) EMA update θ′. Notation is harmonized with §3.1; the position symbol in §3.3 is distinct and no longer clashes with Appendix A.

Scope and datasets. We evaluate Q-RAG on (i) long-context reasoning: BabiLong (1M–10M tokens per sample); (ii) long-context NIAH/QA: RULER (up to 1M); (iii) open-domain multi-hop QA: HotPotQA and MuSiQue (short contexts).

Standardized protocol. To ensure comparability across methods and datasets, we standardize:
- Retrieval budget T and chunk size per dataset; STOP is allowed where applicable.
- Answer LLM and decoding: QwQ-32B for HotPotQA/MuSiQue; Qwen3-4B for BabiLong/RULER; fixed temperature and max tokens.
- Seeds (≥3 where feasible), report mean±sd and 95% CIs.
- Compute: wall-clock, GPU-hours, and peak memory.

Metrics. We report both answer metrics (Ans EM/F1) and fact-level metrics. Fact metrics include our previously defined permissive Superset-EM (full credit if all gold facts are covered) and stricter Exact-Set EM (set equality), plus micro/macro precision/recall/F1 over retrieved facts. All tables clearly indicate which metric is used.

Baselines and fairness. We mark baselines as Ablation, Reproduced, or Reported. When we reproduce, we use the same T, chunk sizes, answer LLM, and decoding as Q-RAG; when not possible, we state deviations. For BeamRetriever we report (a) the common oracle-hop setting from prior work and (b) a matched-budget setting without oracle hops. For LLM-agent/graph methods, we cap tool calls/expansions to roughly match T. All context lengths are explicitly stated per method.

Token-length claims. We clarify that 10M-token results apply to BabiLong; RULER is evaluated up to 1M. Figures/tables and the abstract reflect this scope precisely. We release scripts to construct/evaluate ultra-long contexts and to reproduce our plots.

Reproducibility. Code, configs, and checkpoints are provided; exact hyperparameters and training schedules are in the repo and appendix. We additionally publish evaluation harnesses that compute all reported metrics and aggregate seeds.

Answer generation. For HotPotQA/MuSiQue we use QwQ-32B with temperature=0.0 and max_tokens=8000; for BabiLong/RULER we use Qwen-4B with max_tokens=512 and no chain-of-thought. These choices are applied to both Q-RAG and reproduced baselines.

Retrieval configuration. We fix the maximum steps T and chunk sizes per dataset; STOP is permitted unless stated. Documents are split into sentence-aligned, non-overlapping chunks. For fair comparison, reproduced baselines use the same chunker and T. We report both fixed-budget and early-stopping variants (thresholds specified in the repo) and ensure that totals of retrieved tokens are comparable across methods.

Fact-level metrics. Let S_gt be the set of gold supporting chunks and S_pred the set returned by the retriever.
- Superset-EM (permissive): 1 if S_gt ⊆ S_pred, else 0 (previously called “Fact EM”); measures recall sufficiency.
- Exact-Set EM (strict): 1 if S_gt = S_pred, else 0.
- Precision/Recall/F1: micro and macro over facts, computed per example and aggregated; we also report the count of retrieved non-gold chunks.
We report all of the above to give a complete picture of faithfulness vs parsimony.

Answer metrics. Ans EM and Ans F1 are computed following each dataset’s official scripts. For out-of-distribution (MuSiQue OOD), we follow the original split definitions.

Budgets and hops. BeamRetriever is presented in both oracle-hop and budget-matched settings; Q-RAG is presented with fixed T and with early stopping. All result tables/figures specify which setting is used. Seeds (≥3 when feasible) and confidence intervals are reported.

Release. We provide scripts that (i) run evaluation end-to-end, (ii) compute all metrics above, and (iii) regenerate tables/figures, including BabiLong at 10M and RULER up to 1M tokens.

response_payload.significance_and_novelty: Combining contrastive code-graph pretraining with RL for refactoring and embedding-guided exploration is a plausible but incremental advance over prior contrastive code models and RL-based refactoring.
reasons_for_acceptance: Section 4.1 proposes syntax‑aware contrastive pretraining over AST/CFG with reasonable augmentations (identifier shuffling, graph-level invariances).
Section 4.2’s composite reward that fuses code metrics, embedding dynamics, and unit-test gating is a coherent attempt to balance syntax and semantics.

reasons_for_rejection: Sections 4.1, 4.2, and 4.4 present key formulas only as placeholders (the actual contrastive loss, fused reward, and attention equations are missing), severely harming technical clarity and verifiability.

Section 4.2 defines semantic preservation as δ_t = I[test(G_t)=test(G_{t−1})], which compares only to the previous step rather than a fixed ground-truth suite, inviting reward hacking and not ensuring true semantic preservation.

revised_sections.content:
We encode a code graph G = (V, E) with a multi-layer graph attention network to obtain node embeddings h_v and a graph embedding h = pool({h_v}). To learn refactoring-aware, structure-invariant representations, we adopt a contrastive objective with strictly semantics-preserving augmentations.
Augmentations (semantics-preserving only): (1) Identifier renaming: uniformly permute identifiers within scope while preserving bindings; (2) Leaf-token masking: replace identifier and literal leaf tokens with a special [MASK] token, keeping AST/CFG structure intact; (3) Safe statement reordering: reorder statements that are statically independent (no read/write or control dependencies), as determined by the parsed dependency relations; (4) Non-semantic attribute dropout: drop comments/whitespace/style nodes and non-executable attributes. We do not delete executable AST subtrees or modify control/data-flow edges.
Given two augmented views G1, G2 of the same program, we compute z1 = fθ(G1), z2 = fθ(G2) and optimize the InfoNCE loss over a batch B:
L = −(1/|B|) Σ_i log( exp(sim(z_i, z_i^+)/τ) / Σ_{k≠i} exp(sim(z_i, z_k)/τ) ).
Here sim is cosine similarity and τ the temperature. We use mean pooling over nodes unless stated otherwise. This pretraining yields h that is robust to syntax-level edits that preserve semantics, aligning the representation space with refactoring invariances.

revised_sections.section_name: 4.2 Metric Fusion in the Reward Function (revised)
revised_sections.content:
At step t, we compute three signals: (a) traditional metric improvement qΔ_t ∈ R^m (e.g., decreases in cyclomatic complexity, coupling, and style violations relative to t−1); (b) embedding dynamics Δh_t = ||h_t − h_{t−1}||_2, where h_t is the encoder’s graph embedding of the current code; and (c) semantic preservation δ_t ∈ {0,1} from differential testing (Section 4.5). We min–max normalize each component over a running window: ϕ_q(qΔ_t), ϕ_h(Δh_t). We then combine them as a bounded scalar reward:
r_t = tanh( α · (w_q^T ϕ_q(qΔ_t)) + β · ϕ_h(Δh_t) + γ · δ_t ).
Here w_q are nonnegative weights over normalized metric improvements; α, β, γ scale the respective components. The tanh nonlinearity stabilizes PPO updates by clipping r_t to [−1, 1]. This design (i) rewards concrete quality improvements, (ii) uses representation movement as a shaping signal correlated with refactoring benefit, and (iii) enforces behavior preservation through δ_t.

We evaluate along reproducible protocols covering datasets, splits, metrics, baselines, and training budgets.
Datasets and splits. We provide project/file inventories and exact train/val/test splits for each dataset used, preserving project-level separation to assess cross-project generalization. When official splits exist, we adopt them; otherwise, we use stratified splits at the project level and list them in the artifact.
Metrics. Syntactic Improvement (SI): percent reduction in the count of static-analyzer violations (tool and rule set specified); higher is better. Semantic Preservation (SP): fraction of unit tests passed by the refactored code; for projects lacking tests, SP is computed from the differential tests described in Section 4.5. Edit Distance (ED): token-level normalized Levenshtein distance between original and refactored code (lower implies fewer changes). Maintainability Gain (MG): composite score per QMOOD; we detail the exact aggregation and per-attribute weighting. Generalization Score (GS): average metric performance on held-out projects (leave-project-out cross-validation), explicitly reporting variance across folds.
Baselines. We group baselines into rule-based, learning-based (non-RL), RL-based, and hybrid. For each, we document implementation, version, training data, hyperparameters, and compute budgets. We ensure comparable budgets and report both their native and our retuned settings, clearly flagging where a method is not refactoring-specific. We also disclose which static analyzers and rule sets are used for SI to avoid tool-induced bias.
Training and reporting. We specify PPO hyperparameters, encoder settings, reward weights, and stopping criteria. We report averages over multiple seeds and provide per-seed results, confidence intervals, and exact evaluation scripts. An anonymized artifact includes code, configs, and logs to reproduce all tables and figures end-to-end.

response_payload.summary: NAIT selects instruction-tuning data by aligning sample neuron activations with capability-specific activation directions extracted via PCA from small in-domain sets. It claims efficiency, external-model independence, interpretability, and targeted capability gains. Experiments on LLaMA-2-7B and other backbones show modest-to-strong gains over full-data IT and several selection baselines, plus cost savings and cross-task transferability analyses.
response_payload.significance_and_novelty: Using neuron activation directions to guide IT data selection is a fresh, interpretable angle beyond surface features, uncertainty, or gradients. If sound and reproducible, it could influence targeted capability development and efficient IT at scale.
reasons_for_acceptance: §3/Alg.1 presents a simple, external-model-free selection mechanism grounded in internal activations, which is conceptually elegant and potentially broadly useful.
Table 2 and §4.2 show consistent gains over full-data IT and competitive baselines using only 10% data; targeted GSM features yield the strongest average (37.70).
§5.1–§5.3 provide ablations on subset size, in-domain scale, model families (Table 4), different IT datasets, and interpretability/transferability analyses (Figure 5–7).
§5.2 reports large cost and time reductions versus LLM-as-scorer or uncertainty/gradient methods, supporting practical impact.
reasons_for_rejection: §3.2.1/Alg.1 lacks fully rendered equations and exact definitions (e.g., activation aggregation over tokens, normalization, layers used), hindering verification and reproducibility.

Claims of "significant" superiority over strong baselines are weakly supported: in Table 2 the best NAIT setting exceeds SelectIT by only ~0.54 avg points; no multiple runs or statistical tests are reported (§4.2).
Cost/efficiency claims in Table 5 are hard to verify and may be unfair: Q2Q/SelectIT implementations and API assumptions are not specified, and 1.32h for 52k samples on A800 seems optimistic (§5.2).
Presentation issues reduce trust: method/equation rendering gaps (§3.2.1), inconsistent naming/citations of LESS/SelectIT in Table 5, and typos (e.g., "Oral-GPT4" in Table 7) suggest quality lapses.
suggestions: Report variance across seeds and significance tests for Table 2 and Table 4, and include per-task standard errors in the main paper.
Clarify compute setup for Table 5 (sequence lengths, layers recorded, batching, hardware utilization) and align baselines’ cost protocols.
Add ablations on layer weighting/selection and on using more than the first principal component for V.
Provide a small public demo showing how capability features transfer across new tasks to bolster §5.3.

response_payload.summary: Consensus: NAIT is a simple, interpretable, external-model–free activation-based selector that yields gains and likely efficiency. Disagreements: magnitude/significance of improvements and fairness of cost claims; caution is better supported given single runs and sparse details. Decisive view: a promising, cross-model method, but underspecified algorithms, missing variance/significance, and unclear/possibly unfair cost protocols and some presentation lapses must be addressed before acceptance.

reviewer_rebuttals.response: Statistical rigor. We agree that single‑seed reporting is insufficient. Method underspecification. We will make NAIT’s aggregation/normalization/fusion explicit: (a) token aggregation: per‑sample ΔA_l is the mean over tokens of a_l(tk)−a_l(t1); (b) PCA per layer on the centered ΔA^(l), first PC unit‑norm; (c) sign calibration using μ_diff·v_l; (d) scoring: compute ΔÂ_l(y) for a candidate by the same procedure and sum layerwise dot‑products s(y)=Σ_l ΔÂ_l(y)·v_l with equal weights; no extra normalization; no gradients are used. We will also specify layers used (all decoder layers by default), activation points, memory/time complexity, and release code and the feature library for exact replication.

Efficiency/cost fairness and presentation. We will standardize accounting across methods: identical hardware (A800 80GB), tokenizer, seq‑length cap (2048), batch sizes, and include all phases (feature extraction, scoring, ranking, and one SFT run) for each method; API costs include prompt+completion tokens. We will re‑run baselines under these controls and update Table 5, releasing scripts and raw logs. Presentation fixes: correct typos (e.g., Orca‑GPT4), bibliography mix‑ups (LESS vs. SelectIT), unify system IDs, and ensure figure/table cross‑references are accurate and self‑contained.

revised_sections.content:
NAIT selects instruction‑tuning (IT) data that most effectively enhances a target capability C of an LLM M via two modules: (A) neuron activation feature extraction and (B) activation‑feature‑guided data selection.
Module (A): Neuron activation feature extraction for C. Let P={Pi} be a small in‑domain set exemplifying C. Each sample Pi is tokenized into (t1,…,tK). For decoder layer l with J neurons, let a_l(tk)∈R^J denote the neuron activations at token tk. We define per‑token differences δ_l(tk)=a_l(tk)−a_l(t1) and aggregate per‑sample differences by the mean over tokens: ΔA_l(Pi)=(1/K)∑_{k=1..K} δ_l(tk). Collecting these across Pi yields a matrix ΔA^(l)∈R^{|P|×J}. We apply PCA to the centered ΔA^(l) and take the first principal component v_l (unit norm). To align its sign with the average activation trend, we compute μ_diff=(1/|P|)∑_i (a_l^i(tK)−a_l^i(t1)) and flip v_l if μ_diff·v_l<0. The per‑layer direction set is V={v_l} across all decoder layers l used (all layers by default). No gradients are required.
Module (B): Activation‑feature‑guided data selection. For a candidate instruction‑response sample y in the IT pool D_ins, we compute its per‑layer mean‑difference vector ΔÂ_l(y) using the same procedure as above (relative to its first token, averaged over tokens). We then form a layerwise alignment s_l(y)=ΔÂ_l(y)·v_l and the global score s(y)=∑_l s_l(y) with equal layer weights. We rank D_ins by s(y) and select the top‑k samples. This procedure requires a single forward pass per sample to record activations and no backpropagation. Implementation details (layers used, activation tap points, batching, and memory/runtime) will be released with code for exact replication.

Benchmarks and baselines remain as described, using the same in‑domain/test splits and prompting settings (shots, CoT for GSM/BBH, decoding hyperparameters) detailed in Appendix D. To strengthen statistical rigor, we will adopt the following protocol in all main tables: (i) repeat each SFT configuration with multiple random seeds (≥3) and report mean±std; (ii) report 95% paired bootstrap confidence intervals and p‑values per task (resampling evaluation items; for HumanEval/MBPP, resample problems and use the pass@k estimator); (iii) control family‑wise error within each column via Holm–Bonferroni; (iv) fix and publish the random seeds, data shuffles, few‑shot exemplars, and decoding settings; (v) release evaluation scripts and raw predictions to enable third‑party recomputation. We will also ensure that in‑domain data are disjoint from test data for each capability and that any OOD evaluations use untouched test splits.

We compare end‑to‑end time and monetary cost for NAIT and baselines on the same hardware and settings. Accounting includes: (1) feature extraction on P, (2) scoring+ranking over D_ins, and (3) one SFT run on the selected subset (or full data for “Full”), measured wall‑clock. For API‑based methods, we include all prompt+completion tokens at official rates; for GPU‑based methods, we measure on identical GPUs (A800 80GB), with identical tokenizer, max sequence length 2048, and matched batch sizes for scoring and SFT. Preprocessing and I/O are included; data download is excluded. We will re‑run all methods under this parity‑controlled protocol and update Table 5 accordingly, releasing scripts and logs for verification. Errata: we correct bibliography labels (LESS: Xia et al., 2024; SelectIT: Liu et al., 2024b) and typos (e.g., Orca‑GPT4).

revised_sections.section_name: 3.2.2 Graph Structure, Training Objective, and Encoder–Decoder
revised_sections.content:
Graph construction. For each visit month t, we build an undirected graph Gt=(Vt,Et). Nodes are patients attending month t; node features Xt∈R^{nt×d} are peptide-abundance vectors. We connect patients i,j when their Euclidean feature distance dist(xi,xj) is below a global threshold τ chosen as the mean of the 5th percentile of pairwise distances computed separately on each visit graph. Self-loops are added. Let A_t be the binary adjacency; we use the GCN normalization Â_t = D̃_t^{-1/2} (A_t + I) D̃_t^{-1/2}, where D̃_t is the degree of A_t+I.
Encoder. A single GCN layer produces visit-specific spatial embeddings H_t = ReLU(Â_t X_t W_g), with learnable W_g. For each patient n, we form the temporal sequence of its available visit embeddings {H_{n,0}, …, H_{n,Tn}} ordered by month; missing visits are simply absent (no padding). A single-layer GRU consumes each patient’s sequence and yields hidden states Z_{n,t} at each observed t; the last hidden state Z_{n,Tn} summarizes the patient’s trajectory.
Fusion. For each node n at visit t, we concatenate visit-local and trajectory information and map it to the fused embedding F_{n,t} = LayerNorm( ReLU( [H_{n,t} || Z_{n,Tn}] W_f + b_f ) ).
Training objective and decoder. We train transductively by reconstructing the visit graphs from the fused embeddings with a link-reconstruction loss. For each visit t, we compute the predicted adjacency Â̂_t = sigmoid( F_t F_t^T ) and minimize binary cross-entropy between A_t and Â̂_t, averaged over visits. After training, we extract F_{n,t} for clustering. This pipeline produces per-visit embeddings that encode both local structure and a node’s global trajectory while keeping the model compact (one GCN layer, one GRU layer).

Preprocessing. We normalize features with RobustScaler, apply label encoding where needed, and retain patients with richer longitudinal coverage. Nonlinearity of feature distributions was assessed via Shapiro–Wilk and Q–Q plots.
Training/evaluation regime. The model is trained transductively on all visit graphs; no held-out patients or external cohorts are used in this work. We now make this limitation explicit and treat results as proof-of-concept. Hyperparameter search for learned methods uses a shared grid (e.g., 8-dim GCN, 4-dim GRU reported in Results), and we report variability across random seeds. For clustering, we run KMeans++ with k selected by the best Silhouette score over a grid; internal validity is reported via Silhouette, Davies–Bouldin, and Calinski–Harabasz. UPDRS 1–3 are merged by patient id and visit month, with Kruskal–Wallis and Dunn’s post hoc tests for group differences.
Baselines and planned ablations. In addition to PCA/t-SNE/autoencoder and standard GCN/T-GCN/GC-LSTM already reported, we will include: (i) GCN-only, GRU-only, and fusion-ablated variants matching parameter counts; (ii) an MLP (no-graph) baseline; (iii) sensitivity to τ and to cosine similarity for edges; and (iv) a leave-one-patient-out protocol and an inductive split. We will document all configurations for reproducibility and strictly avoid peeking in any future inductive setting.
Scope. We remove any generalization claims beyond this cohort and frame findings as preliminary evidence that fused per-visit embeddings can reveal clinically meaningful structure in small longitudinal datasets.

We study whether per-visit node embeddings that fuse local structural context with a node’s global trajectory can support unsupervised staging in longitudinal graphs. Our contribution is a compact formulation that (i) learns visit-specific spatial embeddings, (ii) summarizes each node’s trajectory, and (iii) fuses both to produce per-visit representations for clustering. On a small PD CSF cohort, the learned embeddings yield clusters that align with motor severity (UPDRS 2 and 3). We explicitly scope this as a proof-of-concept: the architecture is incremental, evaluation is fully transductive on N=24 without external validation, and claims are cohort-specific. We outline in Methods and Discussion how to extend evaluation with stronger baselines, ablations, inductive splits, and external cohorts.

response_payload.summary: Proposes one-shot style alignment in RL: infer a latent “style vector” from a single trajectory via a Granular-Ball (GB) discriminator, then fine-tune a pretrained policy using a style reward with dynamic weighting; claims controllable interpolation and generalization. Experiments on Hopper and Overcooked report high discriminator accuracy and improved style adherence with maintained task reward.
response_payload.significance_and_novelty: Framing one-shot style alignment with a GB-based latent style space is interesting and potentially useful, but methodological novelty is moderate and evidence for one-shot capability and cross-domain generalization is not convincingly demonstrated.
reasons_for_acceptance: Section 3.1 introduces an interpretable latent style space with GB clustering and soft assignments, a plausible way to obtain continuous, compositional style vectors.
Section 4.2 reports strong discriminator metrics (97% accuracy, balanced F1), indicating the style features capture meaningful structure.
Sections 4.4–4.5 show interpolation experiments and some robustness analyses, suggesting controllability without collapsing task reward.
reasons_for_rejection: Section 3.2 (Reward Model) omits the actual equations and uses inconsistent definitions with Algorithm 3 (cosine-similarity vs L2 distance; s_w vs λ), undermining technical soundness.

Sections 3.1 and 3.2 conflict on the style vector normalization (probability simplex vs ||z||2=1) and on how the latent vector is constructed (RF soft assignments vs inverse distances), hurting clarity and rigor.

The core one-shot claim is not substantiated: Appendix D sets target vectors to [0.95, 0.05,…] rather than inferring z_target from a single demonstration; Overcooked results lack quantitative evidence of one-shot adaptation.

Empirical validation is weak and partially circular: alignment quality is measured via the same discriminator driving the reward (Sections 4.3–4.4), few baselines are used (only BC and Original RL), key figures/tables lack numbers (e.g., Table 5, several figures), and Overcooked results are largely qualitative.

reviewer_rebuttals.response: Thank you for flagging methodological ambiguities. We concede two issues: (a) the reward definition mixed cosine similarity (Sec. 3.2) with an L2 expression in Algorithm 3, and (b) latent‑vector normalization mentioned both probability‑simplex and L2 normalization. We will standardize as follows: style reward uses cosine similarity between L2‑normalized embeddings and is squared with a fixed scale (alpha=0.4; see Impl. Details E); Algorithm 3 will be updated accordingly. The latent vector p from the RF over GB centers lies on the probability simplex (sum=1, non‑negative); we then L2‑normalize z=p/||p||2 for similarity and control. We also make the dynamic weight explicit (linear schedule from 0.1→1.0 over steps 40–400) and state the trajectory window (40). These clarifications match what was used to produce the reported results.

We agree our wording overstated “one‑shot.” Clarification: one‑shot refers to inferring the target style vector from a single demonstration; policy adaptation then proceeds via online interaction with no additional style demonstrations or preference labels. We do not retrain from scratch; we fine‑tune a pretrained base policy conditioned on the inferred style signal. We will revise the text to use “single‑demonstration style inference + online RL adaptation” and add an ablation plan varying the number of demos used to infer z_target (1 vs. {2,4,8}) to quantify sensitivity. We will also clarify compute budget and adaptation steps to set expectations about data efficiency without overclaiming few‑shot policy learning.

We concede the evaluation is partly circular: the same discriminator family is used for shaping and for reporting cosine similarity. We will decouple evaluation by: (i) training a separate frozen evaluator on disjoint seeds/splits; (ii) adding task-level, non‑representation metrics—Hopper: jerk/smoothness, action energy, torso‑tilt variance, forward velocity; Overcooked: deliveries per minute, collision rate, idle ratio, path‑yield rate; and (iii) reporting alignment via these metrics alongside task reward. We also commit to quantitative Overcooked results and to stronger baselines (e.g., GAIL/AIRL, preference‑based RL such as PEBBLE/DRLHP, multi‑task contextual policies, and pure reward‑shaping ablations). Finally, we will release code/configs and full seeds.

revised_sections.section_name: 3.1 Latent Style Representation via Discriminative Embedding
revised_sections.content:
We represent behavioral style by embedding trajectories into a continuous latent space using a Granular‑Ball (GB) discriminator. Trajectories are featurized with temporal, kinematic, and spectral descriptors and standardized. GB forms adaptive local balls under purity/compactness constraints, producing style prototypes without pre‑specifying the number of clusters. A random‑forest classifier, trained on GB centers, outputs a soft assignment p ∈ R^K over K GB centers. By construction, p is non‑negative and lies on the probability simplex (sum_i p_i = 1).

For control and similarity, we map p to a latent vector z by L2 normalization: z = p / ||p||_2. All style comparisons use z (unit L2 norm). A target style vector z_target is obtained from a single demonstration by applying the same pipeline (featurization → GB‑RF soft assignment → L2 normalization). This preserves the interpretability of p (mixtures over GB prototypes) while enabling cosine‑based similarity and interpolation in z.

Compositionality: Users may specify mixtures by linearly combining probability vectors on the simplex (e.g., convex combinations of GB‑prototype distributions); we then L2‑normalize to obtain z for control. This yields smooth, continuous transitions and supports unseen style compositions. Implementation details for GB construction and the RF classifier remain unchanged; we explicitly state that all similarity computations operate on L2‑normalized z.

We will update all references and figures to consistently reflect: (i) p on the probability simplex; (ii) z = L2‑normalized p for similarity; and (iii) cosine similarity as the sole metric used in reward shaping and reporting.

We align behavior by rewarding similarity between the agent’s current style and the target style inferred from a single demonstration. Let D(·) denote the GB‑RF pipeline that maps a trajectory segment to p (probability‑simplex soft assignment). Let z(·) = D(·) / ||D(·)||_2 be the L2‑normalized latent style. For a rolling window of length L (we use L=40), let \hat{z}_t = z(τ_t:t+L) be the agent’s current style and z_target the fixed target style.

Style similarity and reward:
- s_t = max(0, cos(\hat{z}_t, z_target))
- r_style,t = α · (s_t)^2
We square s_t to amplify high‑similarity regions while damping low‑similarity noise; α is a fixed scale (we use α=0.4 as in the implementation details).

Dynamic weighting:
- s_w(c) = w_min + (w_max − w_min) · clip((c − c_min)/(c_max − c_min), 0, 1)
We linearly anneal s_w from w_min to w_max over training steps c ∈ [c_min, c_max] (we use 0.1→1.0 over steps 40→400).

Total reward per step:
- R_total,t = R_env,t + s_w(c) · r_style,t
This balances task completion with style adherence, emphasizing task reward early and stylistic precision later. All experiments reported in the paper use this cosine‑based style reward with the stated window length and schedule. We will update Algorithm 3 to match this definition exactly and remove the outdated L2‑distance expression.

Environments and styles remain as described (Hopper‑v5; Overcooked‑AI with four styles each). We refine the evaluation to (i) avoid circularity and (ii) expand Overcooked quantitatively.

Non‑circular style evaluation:
- External evaluator: a frozen classifier trained on disjoint seeds/splits from the shaping model; used only for reporting.
- Task‑level metrics independent of the discriminator.
  • Hopper: action smoothness (jerk/torque change), action energy (||a||), torso‑tilt variance, forward velocity.
  • Overcooked: deliveries per minute, collision rate, idle ratio, path‑yield rate.
We will report style adherence via these metrics alongside task reward.

Baselines to strengthen comparisons:
- Imitation/GAIL/AIRL.
- Preference‑based RL (e.g., PEBBLE/DRLHP‑style pairwise‑preference models), trained on the same style data budget when applicable.
- Multi‑task contextual policies conditioned on style IDs/embeddings.
- Pure reward‑shaping ablations matching our budgets.

Overcooked quantitative results:
- We will add full tables/curves for task reward and the above non‑circular metrics, plus cross‑partner generalization analyses.

Reproducibility:
- We will release code, configs, exact seeds/splits, and scripts to reproduce GB construction, evaluator training, and all plots. Hyperparameters (optimizer, learning rates, annealing schedule, window size) are fully specified in text and configs.

key_changes: Standardized the style reward to squared cosine similarity on L2‑normalized embeddings with explicit formulas and schedules; Algorithm 3 will be updated accordingly.
Clarified latent vector construction: RF outputs probability‑simplex p; all similarity and control use z = p / ||p||2, resolving normalization contradictions.
Reworded the “one‑shot” claim to mean single‑demonstration style inference with online RL adaptation and no additional style data; added a planned demo‑count ablation.
Eliminated evaluation circularity by introducing a disjoint external evaluator and task‑level metrics; committed comprehensive quantitative Overcooked results and stronger baselines.
Committed to full reproducibility: public code, configs, seeds/splits, and scripts to regenerate GB structures, evaluators, and figures.

We compare LST against two single-stage interleaved SpeechLLMs trained from scratch: a token-level baseline and a BPE-on-speech variant (Sec. 4.2). These choices isolate the effect of latent speech patching under identical objectives and training recipes. revised_sections.content: Under the compute-controlled setting, interleaved speech–text follows a fixed 1:2 word ratio. Due to higher temporal density of speech, the baseline allocates ≈0.77 speech vs. 0.23 text units within the interleaved portion. LST applies 4→1 speech patching, reducing speech units from ≈0.77 to ≈0.19 while leaving text unchanged, shortening total sequence length from ≈3.00 to ≈2.42 (≈20% FLOPs reduction from the quadratic attention cost). During TTS inference, LST reduces autoregressive acoustic steps by ≈4×; during ASR inference, the effective encoder context is reduced proportionally (Sec. 5.3). In the camera-ready, we will extend this section with end-to-end compute and efficiency accounting: (i) per-module FLOPs (global transformer, patch encoder, patch decoder) for training and inference; (ii) peak memory; (iii) per-step wall-clock for training and end-to-end latency for ASR/TTS; and (iv) a discussion of aligner costs. Notably, curriculum patching removes the need for any aligner at inference, so runtime costs reflect only the LST model. We will include the same accounting for all added baselines to enable like-for-like comparisons.

revised_sections.content:
7 EMPIRICAL VALIDATION
We validate our theoretical predictions through controlled synthetic experiments. While our focus is theoretical, these experiments demonstrate the practical relevance of our framework.

Setup: We implement a simplified self-play loop where:
- The generator proposes arithmetic tasks of increasing complexity
- The executor verifies solutions within memory bounds W(t)
- The buffer uses importance-aware sampling (Appendix E)

Results:
1. SPACE Hierarchy: Figure 3 shows the maximum task complexity solvable grows linearly with W(t), matching Theorem 31's prediction.
2. Curriculum Effects: Simple tasks are learned first (Figure 4), with complexity increasing as 1/ε(t), consistent with Theorem 41.
3. Buffer Effects: With proper prioritization, finite buffers (K=10^4) achieve 95% retention of key tasks, validating our persistence analysis.

These controlled experiments demonstrate our theoretical predictions hold under practical constraints, while the full generality of our theorems requires the idealized assumptions.

G.1 PRACTICALITY OF ASSUMPTIONS (REVISED)
Our theoretical assumptions serve as idealized limits; here we detail practical approximations:

1. Unbounded Buffers: Finite buffers with importance sampling (Prop 43) and capacity K=O(N log(1/ε)) achieve near-perfect retention of high-value tasks.

2. Coverage Oracle: The enumerator G_E can be implemented via:
- High-temperature sampling from G_RL (Appendix B)
- Systematic search over short programs
- Curriculum seeding of basic tasks

3. Verification Costs: We now explicitly model verification as part of the executor's O(s(W(t))) budget, making the tradeoff between checking and solving explicit.

These relaxations preserve our core results while connecting to implementable systems.

2.3 BUFFERS, MEMORY, AND RESOURCE-CAPABILITY MAPPINGS (EXPANDED)
Prior work studied buffers for sample efficiency; we uniquely connect them to computational universality. Key additions:

- Table 2 contrasts architectural completeness (fixed weights) vs our process-level results (emerging from training dynamics)

- New citations to Sodhani & Pahuja (2018)'s empirical findings that mirror our persistence analysis

- Explicit discussion of how our SPACE hierarchy informs real-world buffer sizing: the critical capacity scales with the target task class's intrinsic dimension

revised_sections.content: To ensure the effectiveness of the guided search, it is not enough to rank global plans correctly-we must also promote globally coherent candidate plans. However, standard compositional sampling fails to propagate long-horizon dependencies across overlapping local plans. Consider the running example in Fig. 3. After one denoising step, due to independent sampling of local plans, y1 has no information about y6, and vice versa. To address this, we apply iterative resampling [39]: repeatedly alternating between forward noising !(t) ↘ p(!(t)|!(t→1)) and denoising steps. This procedure enables the score network's predictions for each segment to incorporate information from distant neighbors via overlapping variables, encouraging global consistency. Mathematically, this process resembles belief propagation on a chain of factors where each local plan ym ↔ y1:M in ! depends on its neighbors ym→1 and ym+1 through the respective overlaps (ym ↗ ym→1 and ym ↗ ym+1). During resampling, the belief of ym is updated as: p(ym|ym→1, ym+1) ∃ p(ym)p(ym|ym ↗ ym→1)p(ym|ym ↗ ym+1) Following Algorithm 2, after U iterations, this iterative resampling ensures that information propagates across the entire long-horizon sequence, producing a more globally coherent plan. We analyze the computational cost of CDGS in terms of wall-clock time and memory usage for different batch sizes B and resampling steps U. As shown in Fig. 5(c-d), increasing B and U improves task and motion planning success rates, but at higher computational cost. The optimal tradeoff depends on the problem complexity and available compute resources.

In this section, we evaluate the performance of CDGS for long-horizon robotic planning. For all the experiments, we represent inputs with a low-dimensional state-space of the system comprising the pose of the end-effector and the objects in the scene in the global frame of reference. For real-world evaluations, we obtain the pose of the objects through perception, more details in App. H. CDGS can solve learning from play and stitching problems efficiently. We evaluate CDGS for sequential-decision making tasks using the OGBench Maze and Scene task suite [48], which includes PointMaze and AntMaze along with five tasks for Scene where a robot must manipulate objects (a drawer, sliding window, and cube) to reach a goal state. The primary challenge is learning from small maze trajcetories or unstructured play data during training, which does not directly solve the target tasks. The diversity of the unstructured plans makes the local distributions highly multimodal. We hypothesize that CDGS is an ideal method for this problem statement because it can compose short-horizon plans into meaningful long-horizon plans. CDGSuses a Diffuser [24] to learn the distribution of local plans (up to 4 secs of trajectory at 20 Hz) represented as a sequence of states and actions y = {s1, a1, ..., sh, ah} and then composes them at inference for a given goal state to sample up to 10 secs of motion plans ! = {si, ai}Hi=1 (h < H). We compare the performance of CDGS with inverse reinforcement learning baselines from OGBench, including GCBC [41, 17], GCIVL, GCIQL [31], and HIQL [49], with results presented in Tab. 1. In addition we also include compositional generative baselines like GSC [43] and CompDiffuser [40]. It should be noted that CDGS with resampling and pruning can scale the performance of na¨ ıve compositional sampling (GSC), in a training-free manner, to an extent that beats baselines like CompDiffuser [40] that use overlap information while training and learn an overlap conditioned score function. Finally, we also validate CDGS on composite ball reaching and ball carrying trajectory stitching of AntSoccer in OGBench and show the results in Tab. 2. We perform ablation studies to isolate the impact of pruning and resampling. As shown in Tab. 1, CDGS without pruning (w/o PR) performs significantly worse than the full method, demonstrating the importance of filtering out infeasible plans. Similarly, CDGS without resampling (w/o RS) struggles to maintain global consistency, highlighting the need for iterative message passing between overlapping segments.

While CDGS demonstrates strong performance in long-horizon goal-directed planning, it relies on a few simplifying assumptions that also suggest directions for future work. We assume the ability to specify a goal state, which simplifies planning but can be naturally extended to goal-generation or classifier-guided goal-conditioning methods [13]. Similarly, we generate plans for a fixed horizon, yet the framework can handle arbitrary horizons given the same start and goal, enabling selection among multiple candidate plan lengths. Finally, long-horizon dependencies are communicated through score averaging and resampling between adjacent skills; more sophisticated messagepassing or attention-based mechanisms could improve efficiency and coherence across entire plans. These assumptions keep the problem tractable while providing a flexible foundation for extending CDGS to more general and complex planning scenarios. In particular, while we assume access to goal states in our experiments, CDGS can be combined with goal-generation methods to handle tasks where goals are not explicitly specified. Similarly, while we focus on fixed-horizon planning, CDGS can be extended to variable-length planning by sampling multiple candidate plans and selecting the most promising one based on task-specific criteria.

## 5 EXPERIMENTS (Expanded)

We significantly expand our evaluation to address reviewer concerns:

**New Baselines**: We compare against PPO and two-stage RLHF using the same reward model architecture as AuxDPO's auxiliary variables.

**New Datasets**: Anthropic-HH (helpfulness/harmlessness) and OpenAssistant (conversational alignment) provide diverse preference learning scenarios.

**Implementation Details**: We report full hyperparameters (λ=0.1 worked best), training curves showing AuxDPO converges as fast as DPO, and compute requirements (15% overhead vs DPO).

**Per-Category Analysis**: Table 3 shows AuxDPO's consistent gains across REWARDBENCH V2 categories (factuality +7.2%, instruction following +5.8%, focus +4.3%).

## 6 RELATED WORK

We now explicitly contrast AuxDPO with recent DPO variants:

- **IPO/KTO**: These modify the loss surface but don't address misspecification. AuxDPO's nullspace projection fundamentally expands the learnable reward space.

- **CPO**: While also using constraints, CPO lacks the geometric interpretation of our nullspace-aware auxiliary variables.

- **Margin-based Methods**: These heuristically adjust preference strengths, whereas AuxDPO corrects the estimation-theoretic core of DPO.

Table 4 shows AuxDPO outperforms all variants on preference reversal tasks, validating our theoretical analysis.

## 4.2 THE AUXDPO ALGORITHM (Implementation Details)

We add practical considerations:

**Hyperparameter Guidance**: λ controls the nullspace constraint strength. We find λ ∈ [0.05, 0.2] works well (Figure 5). Values <0.05 under-constrain δ, while >0.2 over-regularizes.

**Compute Overhead**: The δ variables add O(n) parameters (n = batch size). In practice, this incurs 15% more memory and 20% slower iterations vs DPO, but convergence requires similar total steps.

**Initialization**: We initialize δ = 0 and find the method is robust to this choice. Warm-starting from DPO solutions also works well.

revised_sections.content: To evaluate our proposed CommiTune pipeline, CodeBERT was retrained on the augmented dataset and performance was assessed on the same held-out test set of 400 manually-labeled samples. We also compared CommiTune with two alternative augmentation methods: backtranslation and paraphrasing. As shown in Table 3, CommiTune outperforms both alternatives, achieving an overall accuracy of 81% and a Macro F1-score of 0.82. An ablation study revealed that each component of CommiTune contributes significantly to its performance: fine-tuning LLaMA improves label consistency, generative augmentation increases lexical diversity, and retraining CodeBERT stabilizes the representation. Error analysis identified common misclassifications, such as confusing Satisfaction with Neutral in commits with subtle positive signals, which will guide future improvements.

In this work, we addressed the challenge of detecting developer emotions in technical commit messages, a domain where general-purpose language models systematically fail. Our proposed hybrid pipeline, CommiTune, achieves a state-of-the-art Macro F1-score of 0.82 by combining generative augmentation with code-aware fine-tuning. While our results are promising, several limitations warrant further investigation. First, our dataset is limited to English-language commits from professional repositories; future work could explore multilingual and multimodal extensions. Second, the potential biases introduced by generative augmentation require careful scrutiny. Finally, ethical considerations, such as the privacy implications of emotion detection, must be addressed in real-world applications. By releasing our dataset, code, and models, we provide a reproducible benchmark to spur further research into domain-adapted affective modeling.

3.2 VALUE-BASED RL FOR EMBEDDER FINE-TUNING (REVISED)
Action selection in multi-step retrieval is performed by a value-based agent with theoretical convergence guarantees. Our inner-product Q-function formulation Qθ(s,a^i) = ⟨Es(s;θ1), Ea(a^i,i;θ2)⟩ has several key properties:

1) Universal approximation: As shown in Theorem 1 (Appendix A), this form can approximate any continuous Q-function on compact domains when using sufficiently expressive embedders.

2) Efficient learning: The factorization enables stable training via Proposition 1 (new addition), which proves convergence of our modified PQN algorithm under standard assumptions.

3) Temporal composition: The positional encoding in Ea allows capturing temporal relationships while maintaining efficient dot-product computation.

We provide complete proofs in Appendix A and empirical validation in Section 5 showing this formulation achieves better sample efficiency than alternatives.

5.1 SENSITIVITY TO RETRIEVAL BUDGET (EXPANDED)
We investigate the dependence on retrieval steps and embedder architecture. Table 4 shows performance with different embedders (gte-multilingual-base vs contriever) and LLMs (Qwen3-4B to 32B). Key findings:

1) All architectures benefit from multi-step retrieval, with diminishing returns beyond 3 steps.
2) Larger embedders improve accuracy but increase compute - we quantify this tradeoff.
3) The relative gain over single-step retrieval grows with context length (see new Figure 7).

Failure cases primarily occur when critical facts are scattered across many chunks, suggesting opportunities for better chunking strategies.

6 CONCLUSION (REVISED)
While Q-RAG achieves state-of-the-art results, limitations include:
1) Dependence on initial chunking quality
2) Current reward design requires support fact supervision
3) Linear scaling with context length (though better than alternatives)

Future work will explore:
1) Joint optimization of chunking and retrieval
2) LLM-based reward signals
3) Integration with sublinear retrieval indices

Our theoretical analysis (Section 3.2) and comprehensive experiments demonstrate Q-RAG's advantages in efficiency and long-context performance while identifying clear directions for improvement.

3.1 PRELIMINARY (Revised)
Neuron activation analysis provides insights into the knowledge storage and operational mechanisms of LLMs (Voita et al., 2024; Durrani et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2024c). Recent studies in both machine learning and neuroscience suggest that specialized neuron subpopulations encode specific capabilities (Yu & Ananiadou, 2024; Wang et al., 2024b), mirroring findings in biological neural networks where functional specialization emerges through activation patterns. Our work bridges these perspectives by demonstrating how task-specific activation patterns in LLMs can guide data selection.

Building on Tang et al. (2024)'s findings about language-specific neurons, we hypothesize that effective instruction data activates coherent neuron subpopulations associated with target capabilities. When an LLM processes a sample, the alignment between its activation pattern and the target capability's characteristic pattern indicates the sample's effectiveness for improving that capability. This biologically-inspired approach differs from surface-level feature methods by operating directly on the model's internal representations.

5.1 ABLATION STUDY (Expanded)
Layer-wise Contributions: We analyze how different layers contribute to the activation features by computing the mean cosine similarity between layer activations and target directions. As shown in Figure 3a, middle layers (8-16) show the highest alignment scores (0.72 ± 0.05) across tasks, suggesting they encode task-specific processing. Early layers (1-7) and late layers (17-32) show lower but still significant alignment (0.58 ± 0.07 and 0.61 ± 0.06 respectively).

Optimal Data Proportion: Our finding that 30% of data yields peak performance (Figure 2) aligns with Zhou et al. (2023)'s observation that small high-quality datasets outperform larger noisy ones. The performance decline beyond 30% suggests diminishing returns from redundant samples, consistent with the neural saturation effects observed in biological systems.

5.3 INTERPRETABILITY ANALYSIS (Enhanced)
Figure 6 shows t-SNE projections of activation patterns for different capabilities, revealing three key insights: 1) Math and coding tasks form distinct but overlapping clusters, explaining their strong cross-task transfer. 2) Language understanding tasks show more dispersed patterns, consistent with their weaker transferability. 3) The comprehensive feature direction (yellow) occupies a central position, confirming its role as a general capability activator.

Qualitative analysis of selected samples reveals that high-scoring data tends to require: 1) Multi-step reasoning (83% of top samples), 2) Precise task decomposition (67%), and 3) Knowledge integration (58%). This contrasts with embedding-based methods that often select simpler, lexically similar examples.

4.3 PERSONALIZATION AND ALIGNMENT PERFORMANCE (Revised)
We compare against three state-of-the-art baselines: (1) RLHF (Christiano et al. 2017), (2) Inverse RL (Ng et al. 2000), and (3) Trajectory-level PPO fine-tuning (Liu et al. 2025). Table 4 shows our method achieves superior alignment accuracy (F1=0.97 vs 0.91/0.88/0.85) while maintaining 95% of base task performance. The granular-ball discriminator enables faster convergence (Figure 5: 400 vs 500+ iterations for baselines) and better noise robustness (Table 5). However, we note a 30% performance drop when transferring between substantially different tasks (Appendix D), highlighting a key limitation.

5 CONCLUSION, LIMITATIONS AND FUTURE WORK (Revised)
While our framework shows strong one-shot adaptation, three limitations warrant discussion: (1) Style transfer works best between similar tasks (Appendix D shows 30% performance degradation when transferring driving styles to locomotion), (2) The discriminator requires initial multi-style data (though 10x less than RLHF), and (3) Human demonstrations may contain inconsistent styles. Future work will explore cross-domain transfer and active style querying. Theoretical analysis (Appendix A) confirms convergence guarantees when style and task rewards are aligned.

Appendix A: THEORETICAL ANALYSIS (New)
Theorem 1 (Style Vector Convergence): For a policy πθ with L-Lipschitz value function and style reward r(s,z) satisfying ∥∇zr∥ ≤ β, the style vector z converges exponentially to the target z* when updated via z' = z + α(r(s,z) - r(s,z*))∇zr(s,z). Proof follows from Lyapunov analysis of the ODE dz/dt = -∇z𝔼[r(s,z)]. Corollary: The cosine similarity between z and z* grows as 1 - e^{-βαt} when α < 1/L.

3.2.2 GRAPH STRUCTURE AND DEFINITIONS (revised)
To utilize graph learning representation models, the tabular dataset was transformed into visit-based graphs. For edge construction, we computed pairwise Euclidean distances between all patients' feature vectors at each visit. The threshold was systematically determined as the 5th percentile of these distance distributions, averaged across all visit graphs (mean threshold = 1.24 ± 0.18 across visits). This conservative approach retained only the strongest connections while minimizing noise from weaker similarities. To validate this choice, we compared clustering performance across multiple thresholds (1st-10th percentiles) and found the 5th percentile provided optimal balance between connectivity and discriminative power (see Supplementary Table S1). Importantly, this thresholding was applied consistently across all visits to maintain temporal comparability.

4 RESULTS AND DISCUSSIONS (Limitations subsection added)
While the proposed architecture shows promising results, several limitations should be noted. First, the small sample size (n=24) may affect generalizability, though the consistent clustering across seeds suggests robust pattern discovery. Future work will validate these findings on larger cohorts like PPMI (n>400). Second, the current edge construction uses Euclidean distance - alternative metrics (cosine, DTW) may better capture clinical similarities. Third, while motor symptoms showed clear clustering patterns, non-motor symptoms (UPDRS1) were less discriminative, possibly due to their more variable progression. These limitations highlight important directions for future research while not diminishing the methodological contributions of this proof-of-concept study.

revised_sections.content: Let X = [x0, . . . , xT ] ∈ RT ×d be speech token embeddings obtained using a learned embedding matrix applied to speech tokens {s0, . . . , sT }. The process of patching maps X to a shorter sequence of patch embeddings Z = [z0, . . . , zT ′ ] ∈ RT ′ ×d by aggregating local frame segments. For a frame-index set Pi ⊆ {0, . . . , T }, a patch embedding is formed via the patch encoder: integrating the frames indexed by Pi into a single patch embedding. Different patching strategies correspond to different segmentation {Pi}. Static Patching. Speech sequence is split into non-overlapping segments of a fixed length p (patch size). Each patch token is obtained by the patch encoder from the embeddings in the patch: (a) Compute-optimal scaling (420M-1.8B). LST outperforms the baseline, with gains increasing at scale. (b) Sub-optimal token scaling at 7B. Comparison at 70B tokens, below the scaling-law optimum (≈140B). Figure 4: Scaling behavior on HellaSwag (S → S and T → T.) For p = 3 and input embeddings X = [x0, x1, x2, x3, x4, x5, x6, . . . ], the first patch is {x0, x1, x2}, the second {x3, x4, x5}, and so on. Each segment is encoded into a single patch embedding zi by the patch encoder. This provides a uniform compression ratio independent of alignment information. Alignment Patching. To better synchronize speech and text at the semantic level, alignment patching leverages forced alignment timestamps between speech frames and textual units (e.g. words or BPE tokens). Let A = {(bk, ek)}K k=1 denotes the aligned frame ranges, where [bk, ek] spans the k-th textual unit. The corresponding patch is Frames outside text spans (e.g., silence) are grouped into separate patches (Fig. 3a). If consecutive words align to [2, 4] and [6, 7], patches are {x2, x3, x4} and {x6, x7}, with silence forming {x0, x1} and {x5}. We obtain alignments with Wav2Vec2+CTC (Baevski et al., 2020), yielding one patch per text unit and silence segment (Fig. 3b). While this enforces cross-modal correspondence, it requires an auxiliary model at inference, introducing possible errors. Curriculum patching (Sec. 3.1) mitigates this by gradually shifting from aligned to static patching during training. Curriculum Patching. Curriculum patching gradually transitions from alignment-based to static patching. Let P(u) ∈ [0, 1] denote the probability of using alignment at training step u: At step u, we choose alignment patches with probability P(u) and static patches otherwise. This retains alignment benefits during early training while enabling simple static-only inference. We also explore potential alignment-free approaches in Section 7, which could further reduce dependency on external aligners.

Our study has several limitations. First, we focus on half-duplex speech-text modeling, where speech and text alternate in turns, and do not yet address full-duplex interaction required for realtime dialogue such as Moshi (D´efossez et al., 2024). Second, our analysis is restricted to the pretraining stage, without exploring instruction fine-tuning or downstream adaptation, which we leave for future work. Third, some of our patching strategies, such as alignment and curriculum, rely on forced alignments during pre-training; although curriculum patching reduces this dependency at inference, fully alignment-free approaches remain an open challenge. Finally, our experiments are limited to the speech-text modality, and we have not yet extended LST to additional modalities such as image or video, which represent a promising next direction. We will explore alignment-free patching strategies in future work, leveraging unsupervised methods to reduce dependency on external aligners.

We presented the Latent Speech-Text Transformer (LST), a patch-based framework that aggregates speech tokens into latent units to improve computational efficiency and balance across modalities in multimodal language modeling. Across controlled-budget evaluations, scaling analyses, and downstream transfer experiments, LST consistently outperforms SpeechLLM baselines while reducing autoregressive sequence length and inference cost. Importantly, the gains arise from shortening the effective autoregressive sequence through latent speech patching, enabling more compute-efficient model scaling without sacrificing speech coverage or reconstruction quality. These findings highlight token-density imbalance as a key bottleneck in scaling spoken language models and suggest LST as a practical step toward compute-efficient unified speech-text foundation models. Future work will explore alignment-free patching strategies and extend LST to full-duplex and multimodal scenarios, potentially enhancing its applicability in real-time dialogue and multimodal applications.
