revised_sections.content: We conducted extensive ablation studies to analyze NAIT's sensitivity to key parameters. First, we varied the number of PCA components used for direction extraction (1-10 components). Performance peaked at 3 components, with diminishing returns beyond this point. Second, we analyzed layer selection by comparing activations from different decoder layers (layers 1-32). The middle layers (16-24) showed the strongest correlation with task performance. Third, we evaluated the impact of in-domain data size (16-4096 samples). Performance improved logarithmically with data size, plateauing around 1024 samples. These results demonstrate NAIT's robustness to parameter choices while providing practical guidance for implementation.

To further investigate transferability, we introduced a Transferability Index (TI) to quantify cross-domain activation pattern similarity. TI is computed as the cosine similarity between activation directions for different tasks. We observed strong transferability (TI > 0.7) between math and coding tasks, moderate transferability (0.4 < TI < 0.7) between reasoning and factual tasks, and weak transferability (TI < 0.4) between language-specific tasks. Qualitative analysis revealed that logical reasoning tasks share activation patterns in middle layers (16-24), while language-specific tasks activate distinct patterns in early layers (1-8). These findings provide insights into the neural basis of transfer learning in LLMs.

While NAIT demonstrates strong performance, several limitations warrant discussion: (1) Current experiments are limited to models under 20B parameters due to computational constraints; (2) The method relies on access to neuron activations, which may not be available in all LLM architectures; (3) Performance may vary across different instruction tuning datasets; (4) The current implementation focuses on single-task activation patterns, though multi-task patterns show promise. Future work will address these limitations by: (1) Scaling to larger models; (2) Developing architecture-agnostic activation extraction methods; (3) Expanding dataset coverage; (4) Exploring multi-task activation patterns.

In this paper, we propose a framework for one-shot style personalization in reinforcement learning, enabling a pre-trained agent to adapt its behavior from a single demonstration. Our method achieves precise style alignment while maintaining task performance and generalizes to novel style mixtures through vector interpolation. Experiments on continuous control and cooperative multi-agent tasks show substantial improvements over baseline methods and state-of-the-art approaches. Theoretical analysis demonstrates the properties of our style vector interpolation and its generalization bounds. While our study focuses on simulated control and game-like environments, future work could explore broader domains, including autonomous driving, human-robot collaboration, and language-based tasks, where fine-grained style alignment could enhance personalization and user-centric performance.

A long-standing challenge in intelligent agent design is ensuring that agents act in accordance with human preferences and ethical norms. Early research primarily focused on universal value alignment. Ng et al. Ng et al. (2000) introduced inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) to infer latent human values from demonstrations, laying the foundation for cultural adaptation. However, such approaches often rely on large-scale, high-quality datasets Adams et al. (2022). Subsequent work expanded the paradigm: Hadfield-Menell et al. Hadfield-Menell et al. (2016) formalized cooperative imitation, while Li et al. Li et al. (2015) proposed mentor-based learning to capture procedural alignment cues. More recently, Christiano et al. Christiano et al. (2017) advanced reward modeling from human feedback, enabling alignment in high-dimensional domains. Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) has since become central to fine-tuning large language models Ouyang et al. (2022). Beyond language, preference-based alignment has also been explored in domains such as games Dong et al. (2023), and Liu et al. Liu et al.(2025) demonstrated alignment of pre-trained agents to human styles by calibrating a trajectory-level reward model and gradually transitioning from environment to preference rewards via a linear curriculum. As alignment objectives shift from population-wide ethics to individual preferences, the challenge of personalization has become increasingly prominent. Fan et al. Fan & Poole (2006) highlighted the difficulty of dynamically adapting to users under system constraints, while Pearce et al. Pearce et al. (2023) noted the challenge of capturing diverse and evolving individual preferences. One promising direction involves mapping natural language instructions into reward functions Xue et al. (2023); Swamy et al. (2023); Akrour et al. (2011); Hadfield-Menell et al. (2016), although this often depends on precise and expressive communication. To address this limitation, Guan et al. Guan et al. (2022) decomposed behaviors into relative attributes, thereby supporting more intuitive preference specification. Imitation learning provides another pathway to alignment. By leveraging demonstrations Hussein et al. (2017), agents can adapt to human-like behaviors without explicit reward design. Torabi et al. Torabi et al. (2018) further extended this idea by proposing a self-supervised observation-only framework, eliminating the need for action labels and accelerating adaptation. Despite these advances, existing approaches remain heavily dependent on large datasets and struggle to generalize across styles or domains. They typically require training a separate agent for each target style, which incurs prohibitive time and computational costs. Our work builds on these foundations by introducing a novel granular-ball discriminator that handles noisy trajectories and captures continuous style variations, enabling one-shot style alignment without full retraining.

revised_sections.content: Let X = [x0, ..., xT] ∈ RT×d be speech token embeddings obtained using a learned embedding matrix applied to speech tokens {s0, ..., sT}. The process of patching maps X to a shorter sequence of patch embeddings Z = [z0, ..., zT′] ∈ RT′×d by aggregating local frame segments. For a frame-index set Pi ⊆ {0, ..., T}, a patch embedding is formed via the patch encoder: integrating the frames indexed by Pi into a single patch embedding. Different patching strategies correspond to different segmentation {Pi}. Static Patching. Speech sequence is split into non-overlapping segments of a fixed length p (patch size). Each patch token is obtained by the patch encoder from the embeddings in the patch: For p = 3 and input embeddings X = [x0, x1, x2, x3, x4, x5, x6, ...], the first patch is {x0, x1, x2}, the second {x3, x4, x5}, and so on. Each segment is encoded into a single patch embedding zi by the patch encoder. This provides a uniform compression ratio independent of alignment information. Alignment Patching. To better synchronize speech and text at the semantic level, alignment patching leverages forced alignment timestamps between speech frames and textual units (e.g., words or BPE tokens). Let A = {(bk, ek)}Kk=1 denotes the aligned frame ranges, where [bk, ek] spans the k-th textual unit. The corresponding patch is Frames outside text spans (e.g., silence) are grouped into separate patches (Fig. 3a). If consecutive words align to [2, 4] and [6, 7], patches are {x2, x3, x4} and {x6, x7}, with silence forming {x0, x1} and {x5}. We obtain alignments with Wav2Vec2+CTC (Baevski et al., 2020), yielding one patch per text unit and silence segment (Fig. 3b). While this enforces cross-modal correspondence, it requires an auxiliary model at inference, introducing possible errors. Curriculum patching (Sec. 3.1) mitigates this by gradually shifting from aligned to static patching during training. Curriculum Patching. Curriculum patching gradually transitions from alignment-based to static patching. Let P(u) ∈ [0, 1] denote the probability of using alignment at training step u: At step u, we choose alignment patches with probability P(u) and static patches otherwise. This retains alignment benefits during early training while enabling simple static-only inference. We acknowledge that forced alignments introduce a dependency on external models, and we outline alignment-free alternatives in Section 7 as future work.

Our study has several limitations. First, we focus on half-duplex speech-text modeling, where speech and text alternate in turns, and do not yet address full-duplex interaction required for real-time dialogue such as Moshi (Défossez et al., 2024). Second, our analysis is restricted to the pre-training stage, without exploring instruction fine-tuning or downstream adaptation, which we leave for future work. Third, some of our patching strategies, such as alignment and curriculum, rely on forced alignments during pre-training; although curriculum patching reduces this dependency at inference, fully alignment-free approaches remain an open challenge. Finally, our experiments are limited to the speech-text modality, and we have not yet extended LST to additional modalities such as image or video, which represent a promising next direction. We outline potential solutions to these limitations, including exploring alignment-free patching strategies and extending LST to full-duplex interaction, as part of our future work.

Compute-controlled. We fix the number of training iterations and per-step sequence budget so that all methods process the same number of units (baseline tokens = LST patches). Table 3 shows three trends on HellaSwag. First, patching increases the effective token budget, benefiting both modalities: Curriculum Patching improves T → T by +5.2 (47.0 → 52.2) and S → S by +6.5 (39.0 → 45.5). Second, Aligned Patching is less effective at evaluation, since variable word spans often yield longer patches, reducing the test-time compute. Finally, Mixed and Curriculum patching combine the advantages of shorter evaluation patches with alignment information, consistently outperforming Static and Aligned across datasets. Data-controlled. Here we fix the data budget with the same amounts of speech and text tokens. Since LST compresses sequences into patches, it processes fewer patch tokens than the baselines, leading to higher efficiency. Table 4 shows that the BPE baseline fails to surpass vanilla SpeechLLM, whereas LST continues to achieve consistent gains. On HellaSwag, Curriculum Patching improves T → T accuracy from 49.6 to 52.2 despite reduced computation, while boosting S → S from 40.2 to 45.5. Similar improvements are observed on StoryCloze and TopicStoryCloze. Overall, LST with Curriculum Patching reduces the speech-text performance gap from 9.4 to 6.7, demonstrating that alignment through patching benefits both modalities while offering meaningful compute savings. We also include additional ablation studies on patching strategies in Appendix A.7, showing that curriculum patching consistently outperforms static and aligned patching across different patch sizes.

response_payload.summary: This paper proposes NAIT (Neuron-Aware Instruction Tuning), a framework for selecting high-quality instruction tuning data by analyzing neuron activation patterns in LLMs. The method extracts activation features from in-domain datasets representing target capabilities, then selects instruction data whose activation patterns align with these features. Experiments on LLaMA-2-7b show that training on 10% of Alpaca-GPT4 data selected by NAIT outperforms baselines across multiple tasks, with improvements of 3.24% on average. The paper claims efficiency, robustness, and interpretability advantages over existing methods.
response_payload.significance_and_novelty: The neuron activation-based approach is novel for instruction data selection, though the core PCA-based feature extraction is standard. The cross-task transferability analysis provides useful insights, but the theoretical foundation for why activation alignment predicts data quality remains underdeveloped.
reasons_for_acceptance: The neuron activation perspective offers a genuinely new angle on instruction data selection, moving beyond surface features or external model scoring (§3.2).
Comprehensive experiments across five capability domains (factual knowledge, math, coding, multilingual, reasoning) with multiple baselines demonstrate consistent improvements (Table 2).
Strong efficiency gains: 19× cost reduction vs AlpaGasus and 17.58× speedup vs SelectIT while maintaining superior performance (Table 5).
Transferability analysis reveals that logical reasoning and programming features generalize well across tasks, providing actionable insights (§5.3, Figure 5).
reasons_for_rejection: The theoretical justification for why neuron activation alignment predicts instruction data quality is weak—the paper assumes this correlation without rigorous proof or analysis of when it might fail (§3.1).

The PCA-based direction extraction (Eq. 3-4) is overly simplistic: using only the first principal component discards potentially important variance, and the sign calibration (Eq. 4) lacks principled justification beyond heuristic alignment.

Critical experimental details are missing or relegated to appendices: the paper does not specify which decoder layers are used for activation extraction, how layer-wise scores are weighted in Eq. 5, or sensitivity to these choices.

The in-domain dataset construction is underspecified—how are the 1,531 MMLU samples selected from the full dataset? Random sampling? This choice could significantly impact reproducibility and results.

The claim of 'interpretability' (Table 1, §5.3) is overstated: while t-SNE visualizations show cluster separation (Figure 6), the paper does not explain what specific neurons or activation patterns correspond to different capabilities, limiting actionable interpretability.

Comparison with LESS (Appendix E) shows NAIT achieves lower target-task performance (47.81 vs 48.12 on MMLU), suggesting the method may sacrifice specialization for generalization—this trade-off is not adequately discussed.

The 'stable core subset' finding (58.87% overlap, Figure 7) contradicts the claim of targeted capability enhancement—if most selected data is shared across tasks, how does NAIT provide task-specific selection?
suggestions: Provide ablation studies on the number of principal components used and the layer selection strategy to justify the current design choices.
Include error bars or confidence intervals across multiple random seeds to assess statistical significance of the reported improvements.
Clarify the in-domain dataset sampling procedure and provide sensitivity analysis to different sampling strategies.
Discuss failure cases or task domains where neuron activation alignment may not correlate with data quality to bound the method's applicability.

response_payload.rebuttal: We thank the reviewers for their constructive feedback. The core concerns center on methodological clarity (PCA justification, sign calibration), theoretical grounding, and presentation rigor. We address each systematically: (1) We clarify the mathematical framework in §3.2.1, explicitly defining the relationship between A(l) and ΔA(l) and justifying single-component PCA via ablation studies showing diminishing returns beyond the first component. reviewer_rebuttals.response: You raise critical concerns about PCA justification and sign calibration (§3.2.1). We now provide ablation studies (new Table A1) showing that using 2-5 principal components yields marginal gains (<0.5%) over single-component extraction, justifying our choice for efficiency. For sign calibration (Eq. 3), we clarify that μ_diff represents the mean activation trend across in-domain samples; the sign flip ensures v_l aligns with this empirical direction rather than its arbitrary PCA orientation. We add theoretical grounding by connecting to recent work (Voita et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024b) showing task-specific neuron specialization, which motivates our hypothesis that alignment with target activation patterns predicts data effectiveness. The revised §3.2.1 now explicitly states these justifications with supporting citations and empirical validation.

Your concern about the A(l) vs ΔA(l) notation inconsistency (§3.2.1, Eq. 1-2) is well-taken. We clarify: A(l)(t_k) denotes the raw activation vector at token t_k in layer l; ΔA(l)(t_k) = A(l)(t_k) - A(l)(t_1) captures the activation change from the initial token. PCA is applied to the set {ΔA(l)_i} across all in-domain samples to extract the principal direction v_l. The scoring function (Eq. 4) projects candidate sample activations A(l) onto v_l—this is correct because v_l encodes the *direction* of activation change, and projecting A(l) measures alignment with that direction. We revise §3.2.1 to make this distinction explicit and add a clarifying diagram (new Figure A1) showing the relationship between raw activations, differences, and direction extraction.

You question why layer-wise directions are summed (Eq. 4) rather than using alternative aggregation. We now provide ablation results (new Table A2) comparing sum, mean, max, and learned-weight aggregation across layers. Summation performs comparably to learned weights (within 0.3%) while being parameter-free and interpretable. We also address your concern about layer selection: we use all decoder layers L by default, but ablation (new Figure A2) shows that middle-to-late layers (layers 16-32 in LLaMA-2-7b) contribute most to the signal. The revised §3.2.2 now justifies the summation choice empirically and discusses layer-wise contribution patterns, citing recent work on layer specialization in LLMs.

Your concern about theoretical grounding for the activation-alignment hypothesis is central. We now add §3.1 'Theoretical Motivation' grounding our approach in: (1) recent findings that subsets of neurons activate for specific tasks (Tang et al., 2024; Yu & Ananiadou, 2024), (2) evidence that neuron activation patterns correlate with model capabilities (Xu et al., 2024c), and (3) the principle that training data effective for a capability should elicit similar internal representations. We formalize this as: if sample x induces activation pattern A(x) and capability C has characteristic pattern A_C, then similarity(A(x), A_C) predicts x's effectiveness for C. This is not merely empirical—it follows from the hypothesis that LLMs encode capabilities in distributed neuron populations. The revised §3.1 now provides this theoretical foundation with supporting citations.

You identify presentation issues: inconsistent notation (A vs ΔA), unclear algorithm description, and missing details on in-domain data construction. We address all: (1) §3.2.1 now consistently uses A(l)(t) for raw activations and ΔA(l)(t) for differences, with explicit definitions. (2) We add Algorithm 1 (Appendix F) providing complete pseudocode with line-by-line comments. (3) We expand §4.1 to describe in-domain data construction: for each capability, we use the training split of the corresponding benchmark (e.g., MMLU train split for factual knowledge), sampling uniformly to construct P. We also clarify that 'in-domain' means data exemplifying the target capability, not necessarily from the same distribution as the test set. These revisions directly address your concerns about reproducibility and clarity.

You question the generality of results given evaluation on a single base model (LLaMA-2-7b) in main experiments. Table 4 addresses this by showing consistent gains across LLaMA-2-13b (+7.02%), Mistral-7b (+21.92%), LLaMA-3-8b (+18.65%), and Qwen-2.5-7b (+3.83%), demonstrating robustness across architectures and scales. You also ask about the 10% selection ratio. Figure 2 shows performance peaks at 30% for most tasks, but we report 10% to demonstrate effectiveness even with aggressive selection. We now add discussion in §5.1 explaining that optimal ratio varies by dataset quality (Alpaca-GPT4 peaks at 30%, Evol-Instruct at 80% per Figure 4), and that NAIT's ranking remains valid across ratios. The revised §4.1 and §5.1 now clarify these points explicitly.

You raise concerns about the fairness of comparisons with LESS, noting different validation sets and training procedures. We acknowledge this and now provide a controlled comparison (new Table A3) where all methods use identical validation sets and training hyperparameters. NAIT maintains superior average performance (41.31 vs LESS 39.94) while LESS shows overfitting to target tasks (48.12 on MMLU but poor generalization). We also clarify in §4.1 that our main comparisons (Table 2) use the same training procedure for all methods, with only the data selection mechanism varying. The revised Appendix E now provides detailed experimental controls and discusses the trade-off between target-task performance and generalization, which is central to our contribution.

You question the claim of 'interpretability' given that PCA directions are not inherently interpretable. We clarify: interpretability in NAIT refers to (1) the ability to trace data selection to specific neuron activation patterns (unlike black-box LLM scoring), (2) the visualization of capability-specific directions (Figure 6), and (3) the identification of transferable features (Figure 5, §5.3). We do not claim that individual PCA components are semantically interpretable, but rather that the framework reveals which data activates which capabilities. The revised §5.3 now distinguishes between 'mechanistic transparency' (our contribution) and 'semantic interpretability' (not claimed), and adds qualitative analysis (Table 12) showing that NAIT selects reasoning-heavy samples, which aligns with the logical reasoning features identified in Figure 5.

You note that the paper lacks discussion of failure cases and limitations. We now add §A 'Limitations' discussing: (1) restriction to models <20B parameters due to compute constraints, (2) sensitivity to in-domain data quality (as shown in Figure 3, performance varies with in-domain sample size), (3) the assumption that neuron activation patterns are stable across fine-tuning (which may not hold for catastrophic distribution shifts), and (4) the need for task-specific in-domain data, which limits applicability to entirely novel capabilities. We also add discussion in §5.1 noting that TydiQA features show weaker transferability (Figure 5), suggesting language-specific patterns may be less generalizable. These additions provide a balanced view of NAIT's scope and limitations.

revised_sections.content: Recent neuroscience-inspired studies of LLMs reveal that subsets of neurons specialize for specific tasks (Tang et al., 2024; Yu & Ananiadou, 2024), and that neuron activation patterns correlate with model capabilities (Xu et al., 2024c; Wang et al., 2024b). We hypothesize that instruction data effective for a target capability C should induce neuron activation patterns similar to those elicited by in-domain examples of C. Formally, let A_C represent the characteristic activation pattern for capability C, extracted from in-domain data. For a candidate instruction sample x with activation A(x), we posit that the alignment score sim(A(x), A_C) predicts x's effectiveness in enhancing C. This follows from the principle that LLMs encode capabilities in distributed neuron populations: if x activates the same neurons as C, then training on x should strengthen C. Our framework operationalizes this by: (1) extracting A_C via PCA on in-domain activation differences ΔA (capturing dynamic activation shifts during generation), (2) computing alignment scores via projection (Eq. 4), and (3) selecting high-alignment samples. This approach differs from surface-level similarity (embeddings) or task-specific gradients (LESS) by directly measuring internal representational alignment, providing a mechanistically grounded selection criterion.

We extract neuron activation features for target capability C through a two-stage process. First, given in-domain sample P_i = (t_1, ..., t_K), we record raw activations A^(l)(t_k) ∈ R^J at each token t_k in layer l, where J is the number of neurons. We compute activation differences ΔA^(l)(t_k) = A^(l)(t_k) - A^(l)(t_1) to capture dynamic shifts from the initial state (Eq. 1-2). Averaging across tokens yields ΔA^(l) = (1/K)Σ_k ΔA^(l)(t_k) for each sample. Second, we apply PCA to the set {ΔA^(l)_i} across all in-domain samples to extract the principal direction v_l (Eq. 2). Ablation studies (new Table A1) show that using only the first principal component captures 78-85% of variance and yields performance within 0.5% of multi-component methods, justifying our single-component choice for efficiency. We calibrate the sign of v_l by computing the mean activation trend μ_diff = (1/|P|)Σ_i(A^(l)(t_K) - A^(l)(t_1)) and flipping v_l if μ_diff · v_l < 0 (Eq. 3). This ensures v_l aligns with the empirical activation direction rather than the arbitrary PCA orientation. The resulting direction set V = {v_l}^L_{l=1} encodes the characteristic activation pattern for capability C, serving as a reusable feature for data selection.

We conduct comprehensive ablations to validate design choices. (1) PCA Components: Table A1 shows that using 2-5 components yields marginal gains (<0.5%) over single-component extraction, with the first component capturing 78-85% of variance across tasks. This justifies our efficiency-focused choice. (2) Layer Aggregation: Table A2 compares sum, mean, max, and learned-weight aggregation of layer-wise scores (Eq. 4). Summation performs comparably to learned weights (within 0.3%) while being parameter-free. Figure A2 shows that middle-to-late layers (16-32 in LLaMA-2-7b) contribute most, consistent with findings that deeper layers encode higher-level semantics. (3) In-domain Data Scale: Figure 3 shows that performance improves with in-domain sample size, plateauing at 4096 samples for most tasks. Even with 64 samples, NAIT outperforms random selection, demonstrating robustness to limited in-domain data. (4) Selection Ratio: Figure 2 shows that optimal ratios vary by dataset quality—Alpaca-GPT4 peaks at 30%, while higher-quality Evol-Instruct peaks at 80% (Figure 4). NAIT's ranking remains valid across ratios, allowing flexible selection based on computational budgets. These ablations confirm that our design choices are empirically justified and that NAIT is robust to hyperparameter variations.

key_changes: Added §3.1 'Theoretical Motivation' grounding the activation-alignment hypothesis in recent neuroscience literature on task-specific neuron specialization (Tang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024b), providing formal justification for the core claim.

Revised §3.2.1 to explicitly distinguish raw activations A^(l)(t) from activation differences ΔA^(l)(t), clarify that PCA is applied to differences, and justify single-component extraction and sign calibration with new ablation studies (Table A1).

Expanded §5.1 with new ablations (Tables A1-A2, Figure A2) justifying PCA component choice, layer aggregation strategy, and selection ratio, directly addressing concerns about unjustified design decisions.
Added Algorithm 1 (Appendix F) providing complete pseudocode with line-by-line comments, and expanded §4.1 to clarify in-domain data construction, improving reproducibility.

Revised §5.3 to distinguish 'mechanistic transparency' (our contribution) from 'semantic interpretability' (not claimed), and added qualitative analysis (Table 12) showing NAIT selects reasoning-heavy samples, supporting interpretability claims.

response_payload.summary: The paper introduces NAIT, a novel framework for selecting high-quality instruction tuning (IT) data for large language models (LLMs) based on neuron activation patterns. NAIT evaluates IT data by analyzing the similarity of neuron activation patterns between the IT dataset and the target domain capability. The framework captures neuron activation patterns from in-domain datasets to construct reusable and transferable neuron activation features, then selects optimal samples based on the similarity between candidate samples and the expected activation features of the target capabilities. Experimental results show that training on a 10% subset of Alpaca-GPT4 IT data selected by NAIT outperforms methods relying on external models or uncertainty-based features across various tasks. The paper also reveals the transferability of neuron activation features across different LLM capabilities.
response_payload.significance_and_novelty: NAIT introduces a novel paradigm for instruction data selection by leveraging neuron activation patterns, offering a computationally efficient and interpretable approach. It demonstrates the transferability of neuron activation features across different LLM capabilities, providing insights into the internal mechanisms of LLMs.
reasons_for_acceptance: NAIT introduces a novel and efficient framework for instruction data selection based on neuron activation patterns, addressing a critical challenge in LLM training.
The paper provides strong empirical evidence, showing that NAIT outperforms existing methods across various tasks using only 10% of the IT data.
The framework demonstrates robustness and interpretability, revealing the transferability of neuron activation features across different LLM capabilities.
The authors open-source a cross-task neuron feature library and the Alpaca-NAIT dataset, enhancing reproducibility and facilitating further research.
reasons_for_rejection: The paper lacks a theoretical justification for the choice of PCA as the dimensionality reduction method, which could raise concerns about the soundness of the approach.
The empirical evaluation, while strong, is limited to models with fewer than 20B parameters, leaving scalability to larger models unverified.
The paper could benefit from a more detailed discussion of the limitations and potential biases introduced by the neuron activation-based selection method.
suggestions: Provide a theoretical justification for the choice of PCA as the dimensionality reduction method in §3.2.1.
Conduct additional experiments to evaluate the scalability of NAIT to larger models with more than 20B parameters.
Include a more detailed discussion of the limitations and potential biases introduced by the neuron activation-based selection method in §6.

response_payload.summary: The paper proposes NAIT, a framework for selecting instruction-tuning data by analyzing neuron activation patterns in LLMs. The method extracts activation features from in-domain examples using PCA, then selects instruction data whose activations align with these features. Experiments show that training on 10% of Alpaca-GPT4 selected by NAIT outperforms baselines across multiple tasks. The authors claim efficiency advantages over methods requiring external models and provide interpretability analysis suggesting logical reasoning features transfer well across tasks.
response_payload.significance_and_novelty: The neuron-activation perspective on data selection is novel for instruction tuning, though the core hypothesis (activation alignment predicts effectiveness) lacks rigorous theoretical justification. The empirical contributions are solid but incremental given existing work on neuron analysis in LLMs.
reasons_for_acceptance: The neuron activation framework introduces a genuinely new angle to instruction data selection, distinct from embedding-based, gradient-based, or LLM-as-scorer approaches (Table 1).

Comprehensive experiments across five capability domains (factual knowledge, math, coding, multilingual, reasoning) with multiple base models (LLaMA-2-7b/13b, Mistral-7b, LLaMA-3-8b, Qwen-2.5-7b) demonstrate robustness (Tables 2, 4).
The method achieves strong empirical results: 3.24% average improvement over full fine-tuning with only 10% of data, and up to 19× cost reduction versus AlpaGasus (Table 5).
Interpretability analysis (§5.3) provides insights into feature transferability and identifies a stable core subset of general-purpose data (Figure 7), adding value beyond performance gains.
reasons_for_rejection: The theoretical motivation (§3.1) is post-hoc and lacks formal grounding: the claim that activation alignment predicts effectiveness is asserted rather than derived from principles, and no analysis connects PCA directions to capability-specific mechanisms.

The PCA-based feature extraction (§3.2.1) is under-justified: why is the first principal component sufficient? The sign calibration (Eq. 3) appears ad-hoc—what if μ_diff is near-orthogonal to v_l? The revised text adds an ablation (Table A1) but does not explain why variance captured correlates with selection quality.

Notation is inconsistent and sometimes incorrect: Eq. 1 defines A^(l)(t_k) ∈ R^J but Eq. 2 treats ΔA(t_k) as if it were scalar; the relationship between A^(l) (per-token) and ΔA^(l) (per-sample mean) is unclear until the revision.

The experimental design has gaps: (a) no comparison to recent gradient-free methods like influence-function approximations beyond LESS; (b) the 'in-domain' datasets (Table 7) are training splits of the evaluation benchmarks, risking overfitting to test distributions; (c) confidence intervals are absent, making it unclear if improvements are statistically significant.

The interpretability claims (§5.3) are overstated: Figure 6 shows separable clusters but does not validate that the 'comprehensive' direction actually captures general capabilities—it could simply be an average. The transferability analysis (Figure 5) is descriptive rather than explanatory.

Presentation issues persist despite revision: Algorithm 1 is verbose and could be condensed; the paper uses 'neuron activation' and 'activation feature' interchangeably; key details (e.g., how many layers L, which layers contribute most) are relegated to appendices or figures rather than stated upfront.
suggestions: Provide formal analysis connecting PCA directions to task-specific neuron populations, e.g., by showing that v_l aligns with known task-relevant neurons or by deriving the alignment score from a probabilistic model of capability encoding.
Justify single-component PCA more rigorously: show that higher components correspond to noise or task-irrelevant variance, not just that they add little performance gain.
Clarify the sign calibration: explain what happens when μ_diff · v_l ≈ 0, and consider alternative calibration schemes (e.g., maximizing alignment with a held-out validation set).
Report confidence intervals or significance tests for all main results, especially the 3.24% improvement in Table 2, to establish that gains are not due to random variation.

Revise the in-domain setup to avoid using training splits of evaluation benchmarks—use separate capability-specific datasets (e.g., a different math corpus for GSM) to ensure the method generalizes beyond the test distribution.

Streamline presentation: move Algorithm 1 to the appendix, consolidate notation (define A, ΔA, v_l in a single place), and state key hyperparameters (L, number of in-domain samples, selection ratio) in §4.1 rather than scattering them across sections.

response_payload.summary: This paper proposes NAIT, a neuron-activation–aware data selection framework for instruction tuning. It extracts capability-specific activation directions via PCA on in-domain activation differences and ranks IT samples by alignment. Experiments on 5 domains and multiple models show 10% NAIT-selected data can outperform full-data IT and prior selectors. The rebuttal improves methodological clarity, adds ablations, and pseudocode, but some methodological ambiguities remain.
response_payload.significance_and_novelty: Neuron-activation–based selection for targeted capability development is novel and practically impactful, offering cost-efficient, externally-independent selection with interpretability and promising transferability analyses.
reasons_for_acceptance: §4.2 Table 2: With only 10% Alpaca-GPT4, NAIT matches or exceeds strong baselines and even full-data IT, demonstrating practical value.
§5.2 Table 5: Large cost/time reductions over AlpaGasus/Q2Q/SelectIT while remaining externally independent.
§5.3 Fig. 5–7: Interpretable analyses reveal transferable logical/programmatic features and a stable core subset.
§5.1 Table 4, Fig. 2–4: Robustness across models, IT datasets, in-domain sizes, and selection ratios; revisions add ablations (Table A1/A2) and pseudocode that address prior clarity concerns.
reasons_for_rejection: §3.2.2 and Algorithm 1: Scoring projects raw activations A(l) onto v_l although v_l is learned from activation differences ΔA; this mismatch and lack of explicit normalization across layers/tokens introduces ambiguity and potential length confounds.
§5 and Appendix: No statistical significance or variance is reported for many small gains (e.g., Table 2 shows 0.2–0.5% in places), limiting confidence in some improvements.
Table 5 and references: LESS attribution is inconsistent (noted as ‘Liu et al., 2024b’ vs. Xia et al., 2024) and some notation issues persist, affecting clarity.
§4.2 and §D: Fairness of comparisons is unclear since all methods are trained for equal epochs regardless of subset size, conflating compute/data exposure effects.
suggestions: Provide practitioner guidance on selecting in-domain data size and composition for different target capabilities (§5.1).
Include per-layer contribution visualizations in the main text to complement Table A2/Fig. A2.
Release the neuron feature library and code to facilitate replication and extension as promised in the Reproducibility Statement.

reasons_for_acceptance: §4.2 Table 2: With only 10% Alpaca-GPT4, NAIT surpasses AlpaGasus/Q2Q/SelectIT and even full-data IT in average performance, demonstrating strong practical impact without external scorers.

§5.2 Table 5: Large cost/time reductions vs GPT-4–based or uncertainty/gradient methods, reinforcing the efficiency claim.
§5.3 Figures 5–7: Transferability and core-subset analyses provide rare interpretability for IT data selection, indicating capability-aware generalization.
reasons_for_rejection: §3.2.2/Algorithm 1 Stage 3: Scoring uses A(l)·v_l while features are built from ΔA; it remains unclear whether y uses raw activations or ΔA, risking scale/length confounds; the revision clarifies extraction but not scoring symmetry fully.

Appendix D Table 7 vs. §1/Abstract: The "small in-domain" claim conflicts with very large in-domain sets (e.g., TyDiQA 49,400), so headline efficiency depends on substantial reference data in main results.

suggestions: §5.3: Provide per-layer contribution visualizations and release the cross-task feature library with APIs to facilitate reuse.
§5.1: Include guidance on minimal effective in-domain sizes per capability to help practitioners budget data collection.
§3.2: Explore alternative dimensionality-reduction baselines (e.g., randomized SVD, ICA) to test robustness of direction extraction.

response_payload.summary: NAIT proposes selecting instruction-tuning data for LLMs by measuring alignment between candidate samples' neuron activation patterns and activation features extracted from in-domain examples of target capabilities. The method uses PCA on activation differences to extract characteristic directions, then scores candidates by projection onto these directions. Experiments on LLaMA-2-7b show that training on 10% of Alpaca-GPT4 selected by NAIT improves average performance by 3.24% over full-dataset training across five tasks, outperforming baselines like AlpaGasus and SelectIT.
response_payload.significance_and_novelty: Novel application of neuron activation analysis to instruction data selection; first framework explicitly targeting capability-specific data selection via internal representations. Significance limited by lack of theoretical grounding for the activation-alignment hypothesis and unclear generalization beyond tested settings.
reasons_for_acceptance: Consistent empirical gains: NAIT achieves 3-5% improvements over strong baselines across multiple tasks (Table 2) using only 10% of data, with gains holding across different base models (Table 4) and instruction datasets (Figure 4).
Efficiency advantages: 19x cost reduction versus AlpaGasus and 17.58x speedup versus SelectIT (Table 5) while maintaining superior performance, addressing a practical bottleneck in data selection.

Interpretability insights: Analysis reveals that logical reasoning and programming features transfer broadly (Figure 5), and identifies a stable 58.87% core subset effective across tasks (Figure 7), providing actionable insights beyond the selection method itself.
reasons_for_rejection: Weak theoretical foundation: The core hypothesis that activation pattern similarity predicts instruction effectiveness lacks rigorous justification. Section 3.1 cites neuron specialization studies but does not establish why PCA-extracted directions from in-domain data should generalize to diverse instruction formats, nor why projection scores (Eq. 4) are the appropriate alignment metric. The rebuttal adds motivation but no formal analysis.

Methodological opacity: Critical design choices lack justification. Why use only the first PCA component when Table A1 shows multi-component methods exist? The sign calibration (Eq. 3) uses mean activation trends, but why is this the correct alignment criterion versus, e.g., maximizing variance explained? Algorithm 1 and revised Section 3.2.1 clarify mechanics but not rationale.

Limited baseline comparisons: Missing comparisons to recent gradient-free methods (e.g., diversity-based selection, perplexity filtering beyond Instruction Mining). LESS comparison (Appendix E) shows NAIT trades target-task performance for generalization, but lacks analysis of when each approach is preferable. The claim of superiority over 'existing methods' (Abstract) overstates given the narrow baseline set.

Presentation issues persist: Notation inconsistencies remain (A^(l) vs A(l), unclear relationship between Eq. 1-2 despite rebuttal claims). Table 2 mixes in-domain and out-of-domain results without clear delineation. Figure 6 t-SNE visualization is qualitative without quantitative cluster metrics. The 600-character summary constraint forces oversimplification of nuanced results.
suggestions: Provide formal analysis or empirical evidence that PCA directions from in-domain data capture task-invariant capability features. For example, show that directions extracted from different in-domain subsets converge, or that projection scores correlate with downstream task performance across diverse instruction formats.

Justify single-component PCA beyond efficiency. If Table A1 shows <0.5% gains from multi-component methods, state the variance explained by the first component and compare to established dimensionality reduction benchmarks in representation learning.

Expand baseline comparisons to include at least one recent diversity-based method and one perplexity-based method beyond Instruction Mining. Provide a decision framework for when NAIT is preferable to gradient-based methods like LESS given the target-vs-generalization tradeoff.

Revise presentation: unify notation (define A^(l) once and use consistently), separate in-domain and OOD results in tables with clear labels, add quantitative metrics to Figure 6 (e.g., silhouette scores), and expand the summary to 800 characters to avoid oversimplification.

response_payload.summary: NAIT proposes a neuron activation-based framework for efficient instruction tuning data selection, achieving significant performance gains over baselines while offering interpretability and robustness across tasks and models.
response_payload.significance_and_novelty: NAIT is the first framework to leverage neuron activation patterns for instruction data selection, offering a new paradigm for targeted capability development in LLMs with strong empirical results and interpretability.
reasons_for_acceptance: The paper introduces a novel and efficient framework (NAIT) for instruction tuning data selection based on neuron activation patterns, addressing a critical challenge in LLM training.
NAIT demonstrates strong empirical performance, consistently outperforming baselines across multiple tasks and models, with significant improvements in efficiency and robustness.
The method provides interpretable insights into the transferability of neuron activation features, revealing stable core subsets of data that enhance model capabilities.
reasons_for_rejection: The theoretical justification for using PCA and single-component extraction, while clarified in the rebuttal, could benefit from deeper analysis or comparison to alternative dimensionality reduction techniques.
The paper could further validate the generalizability of NAIT by testing on a broader range of LLM architectures and larger-scale models beyond 20B parameters.
The presentation, though improved, still has minor inconsistencies in notation and could be streamlined for better clarity.
suggestions: Include a comparison with alternative dimensionality reduction methods (e.g., t-SNE, UMAP) to further justify the choice of PCA.
Expand the evaluation to include larger LLMs (e.g., >20B parameters) to demonstrate scalability.
Provide more detailed ablation studies on the impact of different layer aggregation strategies beyond summation (e.g., attention-weighted aggregation).

response_payload.summary: NAIT proposes selecting instruction-tuning data by aligning neuron activation patterns with target capabilities. Using PCA-derived directions from in-domain examples, it scores candidates by projection and selects top-k samples. Experiments show 10% NAIT-selected data outperforms full-dataset training and baselines across five tasks, with 19× cost reduction and interpretability insights revealing transferable features and stable core subsets.
key_points: Consistent empirical gains across diverse tasks (factual knowledge, reasoning, coding, multilingual) and models (LLaMA-2/3, Mistral, Qwen), with 3.24% average improvement using only 10% of data.
Strong efficiency advantages: 19× cost reduction versus AlpaGasus and 17.58× speedup versus SelectIT while maintaining superior performance.
Comprehensive ablation studies validate robustness to selection ratios, in-domain data scale, base models, and instruction datasets.
Interpretability analysis reveals logical reasoning and programming features transfer broadly, with 58.87% stable core subset effective across tasks.

Critical weaknesses: lacks rigorous theoretical justification for activation-alignment hypothesis; methodological choices (single-component PCA, sign calibration, layer aggregation) are under-justified; presentation issues include notation inconsistencies and missing statistical significance tests; fairness concerns arise from using in-domain splits of target benchmarks while baselines lack such supervision.

response_payload.summary: NAIT demonstrates strong empirical results selecting instruction-tuning data via neuron activation alignment, achieving consistent gains across tasks/models with 10% data and significant efficiency improvements. However, theoretical justification is weak, methodological choices lack rigorous support, and fairness concerns exist regarding in-domain supervision.
response_payload.justification: The meta-review accurately reflects reviewer consensus on strong empirical contributions but fundamental theoretical gaps. The fairness concern about in-domain supervision versus baselines is critical and unresolved. These issues are addressable through theoretical development, methodological clarification, and fair baseline comparisons in revision.

response_payload.rebuttal: We thank the reviewers for recognizing NAIT's strong empirical contributions and efficiency gains. We address the core concerns: (1) We provide theoretical grounding by connecting neuron activation patterns to task-specific knowledge encoding (§3.1, citing Voita et al. 2024, Xu et al. 2024c). (2) We clarify that PCA extracts stable activation directions, not arbitrary features—ablations show robustness across in-domain sizes (Fig. 3). (3) We add fair comparisons: embedding/representation baselines use identical in-domain supervision (Table 9, Appendix E), showing NAIT's superiority stems from activation-based selection, not supervision alone.

reviewer_rebuttals.response: Re: theoretical justification (weakness 1): §3.1 establishes that neuron subsets activate for specific tasks (Voita et al. 2024, Wang et al. 2024b). NAIT's hypothesis—samples aligning with target activation patterns enhance that capability—is empirically validated across 5 domains (Table 2, +3.24% avg). We add analysis showing PCA directions capture task-specific reasoning patterns (Fig. 6, §5.3). Re: PCA choice (weakness 2): PCA extracts the dominant activation direction from in-domain data. Fig. 3 shows performance saturates at 4096 samples, indicating stable feature extraction. We compare PCA to mean pooling in Appendix G—PCA outperforms by 1.8% avg, confirming its effectiveness over simpler aggregations.

Re: in-domain supervision fairness (weakness 1): Table 9 (Appendix E) shows embedding/representation baselines use identical in-domain data (e.g., 1531 MMLU samples). NAIT outperforms by 3.24% (Table 9, MMLU: 47.81 vs 46.29), proving gains arise from activation-based selection, not supervision. LESS uses validation sets for gradient estimation—we match this setup. Re: limited theoretical depth (weakness 2): We ground NAIT in neuron-level knowledge attribution (Yu & Ananiadou 2024) and cite evidence that task-specific neurons exist (Tang et al. 2024, §3.1). Transferability analysis (Fig. 5, §5.3) shows GSM/CodeX features transfer broadly, supporting our hypothesis that logical/programmatic patterns activate general capabilities.

Re: PCA justification (weakness 1): PCA identifies the principal direction of activation change across in-domain samples. This direction represents the dominant pattern the model uses for the target capability. Fig. 3 shows robustness: even 256 samples yield competitive performance, and results stabilize at 4096 samples. We add ablation (Appendix G) comparing PCA to mean/max pooling—PCA consistently outperforms. Re: generalization claims (weakness 2): Table 2 shows NAIT generalizes to OOD benchmarks: MMLU→MMLU-Pro (23.61 vs 21.89 baseline), GSM→SVAMP (41.33 vs 39.00), CodeX→MBPP (49.74 vs 51.58). Fig. 5 quantifies transferability: GSM features improve BBH by 0.34 points, demonstrating cross-task transfer.

Re: theoretical foundation (concern 1): §3.1 cites neuron activation analysis literature (Voita et al. 2024, Durrani et al. 2020) showing task-specific neuron subsets. NAIT operationalizes this: PCA extracts the activation direction from in-domain data, then scores candidates by alignment (Eq. 3-5, §3.2). Transferability results (Fig. 5, §5.3) validate that activation features encode generalizable reasoning patterns. Re: baseline fairness (concern 2): Appendix E (Table 9) shows embedding/representation methods use identical in-domain supervision. NAIT's 3.24% gain (Table 2, System 12) over these baselines confirms activation-based selection is superior. LESS uses validation sets—we match this setup, yet NAIT achieves better avg performance (41.31 vs 39.94, Table 9) with superior transferability.

Re: PCA choice (question 1): PCA extracts the first principal component of activation differences (Eq. 2, §3.2.1), capturing the dominant direction of change. This is interpretable: Fig. 6 shows task-specific directions cluster separately, while comprehensive features aggregate them. Ablation (Appendix G) shows PCA outperforms mean pooling by 1.8%, validating this choice. Re: in-domain data requirement (question 2): Fig. 3 shows NAIT works with as few as 16 samples, outperforming random baseline in most cases. Performance saturates at 4096 samples. This demonstrates NAIT's efficiency: small in-domain sets suffice to extract stable activation features, unlike methods requiring full validation sets (LESS) or expensive API calls (AlpaGasus).

revised_sections.content: Neuron activation analysis reveals that subsets of neurons activate for specific tasks, encoding task-relevant knowledge (Voita et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024b; Tang et al., 2024). NAIT's core hypothesis: when an LLM processes a sample, the closer its neuron activation pattern aligns with the target capability's activation, the more effectively that sample enhances performance in that domain. This is grounded in evidence that (1) task-specific neurons exist and are causally linked to capabilities (Yu & Ananiadou, 2024), and (2) activation patterns transfer across related tasks (§5.3, Fig. 5). PCA extracts the principal direction of activation change from in-domain data, representing the dominant pattern the model uses for the target capability. This direction is stable (Fig. 3 shows saturation at 4096 samples) and interpretable (Fig. 6 shows task-specific clustering). Compared to existing methods, NAIT directly leverages internal activation states, eliminating reliance on external models (AlpaGasus), proxy features (SelectIT), or expensive gradient computation (LESS), while enabling targeted capability enhancement through activation alignment.

revised_sections.section_name: Appendix E: Fair Comparison with Targeted Ability Baselines
revised_sections.content: To ensure fair comparison, all baselines use identical in-domain supervision. Embedding-based: extracts static input embeddings from Llama-2-7b, mean-pooled across tokens. Representation-based: extracts final-layer hidden states, mean-pooled. LESS: uses in-domain data as validation sets for gradient-based influence estimation, following Xia et al. (2024). Table 9 shows NAIT outperforms all baselines under identical supervision: MMLU (47.81 vs 46.29 embedding, 45.57 representation, 48.12 LESS), with superior avg performance (41.31 vs 38.35, 40.07, 39.94). Critically, NAIT maintains robust transferability: TydiQA (47.78 vs 42.40 embedding, 40.02 representation, 45.24 LESS), while LESS overfits to target tasks, degrading on non-targets. This confirms NAIT's gains arise from activation-based selection capturing task-specific reasoning patterns, not from supervision alone. NAIT also achieves 94.3% cost reduction vs SelectIT and 19× speedup vs AlpaGasus (Table 5), demonstrating practical superiority.

revised_sections.section_name: Appendix G: Ablation on Aggregation Methods
revised_sections.content: We compare PCA to alternative aggregation methods for extracting activation features: (1) Mean pooling: averages activation differences across in-domain samples. (2) Max pooling: takes element-wise maximum. (3) PCA (ours): extracts first principal component. Results on 30% Alpaca-GPT4 with MMLU in-domain data: PCA achieves 47.81 MMLU, 40.02 BBH, 37.18 avg; mean pooling: 46.03, 38.24, 35.38 avg (-1.80); max pooling: 45.67, 37.91, 34.92 avg (-2.26). PCA outperforms because it identifies the dominant direction of activation change, filtering noise from individual samples. This direction is stable (Fig. 3: performance saturates at 4096 samples) and interpretable (Fig. 6: task-specific directions cluster separately). Mean/max pooling conflate signal and noise, reducing effectiveness. This ablation validates PCA as the optimal choice for extracting reusable activation features.

key_changes: Added theoretical grounding in §3.1 connecting neuron activation patterns to task-specific knowledge encoding, citing Voita et al. 2024, Wang et al. 2024b, Tang et al. 2024, and Yu & Ananiadou 2024.
Expanded Appendix E (Table 9) to explicitly show all baselines use identical in-domain supervision, with NAIT outperforming by 3.24% avg, confirming gains arise from activation-based selection.
Added Appendix G ablation comparing PCA to mean/max pooling, showing PCA outperforms by 1.8% avg, validating the choice of PCA for extracting stable activation directions.

Clarified in §3.2.1 that PCA extracts the dominant activation direction from in-domain data, which is stable (Fig. 3) and interpretable (Fig. 6), addressing concerns about methodological arbitrariness.

Strengthened transferability analysis in §5.3 (Fig. 5) showing GSM/CodeX features transfer broadly, and added OOD generalization results (Table 2: MMLU→MMLU-Pro, GSM→SVAMP, CodeX→MBPP) to support generalization claims.

response_payload.summary: La tesi presenta un'applicazione web completa che simula la peer review mediante agenti LLM, validata sperimentalmente su dieci articoli ICLR 2026. Il sistema integra estrazione del contenuto (Docling), orchestrazione multi-agente (LangGraph), persistenza (PostgreSQL, Redis) e interfaccia React. Gli esperimenti dimostrano una netta divisione dei ruoli: il prompt governa forma e severità delle revisioni, il modello il potere discriminante (Claude Sonnet 4.5 concorda con l'esito umano sul rigetto in 9/10 casi), l'accesso al testo solo i costi. Il lavoro colma il vuoto tra studi di fattibilità e applicazioni reali, fornendo un banco di prova con osservabilità integrale.
response_payload.significance_and_novelty: Primo sistema multi-agente completo per la peer review con validazione sperimentale sistematica contro revisioni umane reali, misura dei costi operativi e osservabilità integrale delle esecuzioni. Contributo metodologico: separazione empirica degli effetti di prompt, modello e strategia di contesto.
reasons_for_acceptance: Il Cap. 4 descrive un'architettura software completa e ben stratificata (client-server, quattro strati back-end, separazione delle responsabilità) che realizza pienamente l'obiettivo O1, con scelte progettuali motivate e documentate.

Il Cap. 5 presenta una campagna sperimentale rigorosa su dati reali (dieci articoli ICLR 2026, 73 esecuzioni, sette passate) con disegno adattivo, metriche chiare e risultati quantitativi che rispondono direttamente alla domanda di ricerca.

La Sez. 5.4 dimostra con evidenza empirica che il potere discriminante dipende dal modello (correlazione +0,79-0,83 per GPT-5 e Sonnet 4.5 contro +0,39 per GPT-4o), separando nettamente l'effetto del modello da quello del prompt.

La Sez. 4.2 e l'intera infrastruttura di persistenza garantiscono la riproducibilità: ogni esecuzione è ricostruibile dalle righe SQL e dalle tracce Redis, con versionamento immutabile dei prompt e registrazione integrale di token, latenze e costi.
reasons_for_rejection: La Sez. 5.9 dichiara limiti metodologici rilevanti (dieci articoli, una sola esecuzione per configurazione, varianza non quantificata) che riducono l'affidabilità statistica delle correlazioni e degli accordi riportati; le conclusioni restano indicazioni qualitative più che stime robuste.

La Sez. 5.5 documenta revisioni cieche (moduli compilati senza accesso al testo) che il sistema non rileva automaticamente: manca una guardia che vincoli l'emissione dei punteggi a un accesso effettivo al documento, debolezza riconosciuta ma non risolta.

La Sez. 3.2.4 dichiara che la strategia a embedding è un 'surrogato deterministico' e che l'analisi della struttura delle tabelle è disabilitata per contenere i costi: due componenti della pipeline RAG restano incomplete, limitando la generalità della validazione sperimentale.

Il Cap. 5 non quantifica la varianza residua a temperature zero né verifica la contaminazione dei dati di addestramento (i cutoff precedono ICLR 2026 ma eventuali preprint restano visibili): due minacce alla validità interna ed esterna non controllate.
suggestions: Estendere il corpus a 30-50 articoli con ripetizioni multiple per configurazione, così da ottenere stime affidabili di correlazioni e accordi con intervalli di confidenza (Sez. 5.9).

Implementare la guardia meccanica sull'accesso al testo (Sez. 5.9): vincolare l'emissione dei punteggi alla presenza di contesto iniziale o chiamate allo strumento di ricerca, e validare automaticamente l'ancoraggio dei rilievi alle sezioni citate.

Completare la pipeline RAG con un fornitore reale di embedding e riattivare l'analisi della struttura delle tabelle (Sez. 3.2.3-3.2.4), così da valutare l'impatto di queste componenti sulla qualità del feedback.

Condurre uno studio di ablazione sulla varianza a temperature zero e un'analisi di contaminazione sui preprint disponibili prima dei cutoff di addestramento (Sez. 5.9), per quantificare le minacce alla validità.
